...has come) to repeat certain matters somewhat more deeply and thoroughly.

->Chrisophilus.<-

Yes, I have been waiting for that for a long time; speak forth.

->Theophrastus.<-

First, you should consider and esteem that the **alchemical art** <term>Alchimistische Kunst; the practice of transforming base matter and seeking the "philosopher's stone."</term> is the most ingenious of all arts. Likewise, it is of the greatest use and even necessity to the human race. Therefore, it is (as you will hereafter understand) not unworthy for a man to spend his entire life with and within it. However, it is far more extensive than you might suspect; for that reason, we should hold and value the entire art—both that which deals with **metals** and that which concerns other **minerals**—as consisting of a twofold difference or distinction.

The first is that which has sprung from natural principles or origins. It arises from the cause of equal communication or harmonious agreement, and from the opposition of two natures which are set against one another; this is highly to be praised and wondered at.

The other, however, wishes to be regarded as such—or rather, it would prefer to be held as such than to actually be it—and for that reason, it is **sophistical** <note>In this context, "sophistical" refers to false or fraudulent alchemy that uses trickery to mimic results.</note> and deceptive. Its outcome and end, because it is deceitful, has never been desired by any wise man; yet by those who possess the same level of understanding as the common **rabble** <note>original: "Pöfel"; referring to the uneducated or those easily fooled by appearances.</note>, it is accepted as good by almost everyone. The other <insert>true</insert> **alchemy** is accustomed to bringing forth wonderful, very beautiful, and also healing—not to mention divine—**effects** <term>Würckungen; the practical results or operations of a chemical process.</term> from the secrets of nature (as I have mentioned). Certain things have been conquered and discovered through this same art by ingenious people, but they have come into common use to such an extent that they are no longer worthy of being called "art." However, certain effects of this art have indeed not yet been discovered, of which there are a great number...

But that same first matter, when it is prepared and ready for birth, exists as a potential <note>original: "*potentia*"; the capacity to become something else.</note> or power; yet in itself, it is already an effect <note>The author distinguishes between matter's *potential* to become something and its *actual* existence as a substance.</note>. However, as it is loved and grasped by the Form <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "Form" is the organizing principle that gives matter its specific identity (e.g., making matter into "gold" or "lead").</note> to which it is then subject, it gains dominion. And it must also be noted that this same first matter does not renounce all things in vain, but also keeps within itself a certain quantity <note>original: "*Quantitet*"</note>, which the **Philosophers** have called infinite. 

Even though these things are quite obvious, you and your deceivers have preferred to remain thoughtless. That which natural reason has ordained to be suitable for the first matter, you instead ordain to the fire for burning and roasting. You cannot deny that you wish to bring about all these births through fire, yet neither fire nor its element is suited for this purpose. Fire cannot and may not "give birth"; rather, an artist alone tries to produce something from the outside, while the first matter alone, from within, awakens and sustains all things.

# A Dialogue on Alchemy.

...to cook **mercury** and **arsenic**, so that in the very practice which is otherwise useful for human necessity, he brings about or causes swift death as his own payment. If you should ever encounter someone to whom all the secrets of this art might be revealed (the likes of whom I believe exist nowhere), it seems to me in no way consistent with the truth that he would teach you the true secrets of the art. For it is sufficiently obvious what trickery powerful lords ultimately use against those from whom they learn hidden arts, and what kind of reward they pay and return to them for their immeasurably great toil and labor. It would only be because they preferred to be magnificently and gloriously miserable, and to always consume something praiseworthy while in **golden leg-irons** <note>This refers to the historical reality where successful or promising alchemists were kept as "court captives" by princes. They lived in luxury but were forbidden from leaving, often under threat of death, so the patron could maintain a monopoly on their supposed gold-making.</note>.

I will not deny that the darkness of the mind can be dispelled through the company of experienced and learned people, as far as all kinds of excellent arts are concerned. This is something that **Socrates** himself acknowledges: namely, that he never taught the art to anyone, but only acted like a physician, who does not give sight to the blind, but only wipes away the darkness from them. If the sharpness of sight is then directed and suited toward its object, so it also happens with other arts. That this also holds true and applies to the perfect knowledge of our **alchemical** art is well known to the wise. 

This art, while quite easy (for those who wish to become rich and desire nothing higher than wealth), is yet the most difficult. But that riches should be the rewards of wisdom—riches which are joined with wondrous and manifold tribulations and are subject to the mockery or the hunt <note>original: "Jazung" – a variant of the word for "chase" or "pursuit," implying that fortune constantly harasses the wealthy.</note> of fortune—no sensible person will admit; therefore, such riches are not to be desired. And although this is so, the intemperance of men, the lack of wisdom, and the stubbornness of desires—yes, like raging horses—plunge...

Remove the <term>receiver</term> <note>original: "Receptacul"; the vessel used to catch the distillate.</note> as well and keep it separate; do not add it to the first distillates, as it is not useful for the work. Then, put another receiver in place; then a poor water will come over, but in large drops. <term>Distill</term> <note>original: "distilier"; the process of heating a liquid to create vapor and then cooling that vapor back into a liquid to purify it.</note> this with a gentle fire until a substance remains at the bottom like thin, melted honey. [Repeat this] until you have four measures of this earth, and you should always combine them. You shall distill this until you have eight measures of the good <term>spirits</term> <note>original: "Spiritus"; the volatile, alcoholic essence of the wine.</note> of the earth; you shall distill it until it has no more water with it and is completely separated; then it is correct.

Then take it out of the heat and pour off the spirit very carefully so that no earth flows out with it. For the sake of safety, distill it through a <term>filter</term> <note>original: "Filtrum"</note>. Put this into a <term>distilling vessel</term> <note>original: "Distillatorium"</note> and place it in a water bath; distill the spirit off through the water bath so that the earth remains thick like honey. # To make the Air.

Take this aforementioned <term>Earth</term> <note>original: "Terram"; the solid residue or "body" remaining after the first distillation.</note>, put it into a <term>retort</term> <note>original: "Scheidkrůg"; a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling liquids.</note>, and set it in a <term>sand bath</term> <note>original: "Sandt"; a container of sand heated from below to provide an even, dry heat.</note>, and distill an <term>Oil</term> <note>original: "Oleum"; in alchemy, an "oil" is a concentrated, viscous liquid extracted from a substance, often seen as its essential soul.</note> that floats upon all waters. You shall distill it for so long until you see that your **Black Earth** is fixed; you shall do this until your Earth becomes quite dry, <note>original: "vt sequitur"; Latin for "as follows".</note>. And from this Oil, the **Air** is made by <term>rectifying</term> <note>original: "rectificieren"; the process of purifying a substance by distilling it repeatedly.</note> the Oil.

# To make the Fire.

You shall take the **Fixed Black Earth** and pour its <term>Spirit</term> <note>original: "Spiritum"; the volatile essence.</note>, which was distilled before, upon it, if you wish to have a <term>coagulated quintessence</term> <note>original: "coagulierte quintam essentiam"; the "fifth element" or purest essence of a substance, brought into a solid or semi-solid form.</note>. But if you wish only to distill the **Fire** first, then pour your distilled Oil upon it, and <term>putrefy</term> <note>original: "putrificier"; to let a substance rot or digest at a gentle heat to break down its structure.</note> it for 14 days in <term>horse dung</term> <note>original: "Equino" (likely shorthand for *venter equinus*); alchemists used the natural, steady heat of a fermenting dung heap as a primitive incubator.</note>, so that whatever of the Fire is in the Earth may be drawn out of it. Then distill an Oil again; this is quite fatty and floats on top. Pour that same oil back onto the Earth and set it to putrefy in dung for 14 days as before. Then distill the Fire out of the Earth, dry it as before, and set it out in the open air. If you see that the Earth would <term>dissolve</term> <note>original: "soluieren"; specifically deliquescence, where a salt absorbs enough moisture from the air to become liquid.</note> in the air, then pour the Spirit that was distilled earlier back upon or over it, and distill it yet again. [Distill] an Oil, which is Fire, and keep the Earth. Add that to the previous Earth, and every time you shall test your Earth in the air to see if it becomes moist and yet does not dissolve. You must always pour the distilled Fire upon it and do this until you see that the Earth remains completely dry in the air; then it is correct.

Also, the Oil that is distilled from the Earth for the first time should be used to rectify the **Air**, so that it becomes volatile like a smoke; and in that Oil, **Gold** <note>original: "$\odot$"; the alchemical symbol for the Sun and Gold.</note> is made into an Oil that floats upon that same Oil, and it is called [the Oil] **of the Philosophers** <note>original: "Philosophorum".</note>.

# The method of sowing the seed into the earth.

Take the <term>amalgam</term> <note>A mixture of mercury with another metal, in this case, gold.</note> of <term>Mercury</term> <note>original symbol: ☿</note> and <term>Gold</term> <note>original symbol: ☉</note>; place it in a <term>cucurbit</term> <note>A gourd-shaped glass vessel used as the base of a distillation apparatus.</note>, well <term>luted</term> <note>original: "verluttiert"; sealed with a paste or clay to make the vessel airtight.</note>, in warm ashes. Take of the water or fire in which this Mercury is prepared for the <term>tincture</term> <note>A potent alchemical substance capable of transforming or "tinging" base metals into noble ones.</note>, and of the earth.

The fire is either:
- Warm,
- Cold,
- Moist,
- or Dry.

The enduring fire is the soul; it <term>tinges</term> <note>To "tinge" is to imbue a substance with new properties or to transform its essence through alchemical coloring.</note> and makes the Mercury fluid and penetrating into the metals; it also unites the Mercury with Gold so that they can no longer be separated, and these three things become one thing:

- The Body of Gold,
- The Spirit of Mercury,
- The <term>Animax Animaxini</term> <note>A term likely referring to the "soul of souls" or a highly refined essence.</note>, which is the soul of wine.

The enduring fire increases the metals, and without this fire, the Art cannot be performed.

### Preparation of the Water.

Take the best wine and distill it so many times that if a cloth is soaked in it and lit, the cloth burns away entirely. This wine is called "the water" and the <term>quintessence</term> <note>original: "fünffte Wesenheit"; the pure, concentrated fifth essence of a substance, beyond the four physical elements.</note>; give this water its spirit.

The spirit of the burning water is the spirit of <term>Aqua Fortis</term> <note>original: "Spiritus Aquæ-fortis"; literally "strong water," a corrosive mineral acid, typically nitric acid.</note>.

# Of the Green Lion.

...into a retort / place it in a sand bath / give it gentle fire until the moisture passes away / then strengthen the fire / so the **green lion** <note>In alchemy, the "Green Lion" often refers to vitriol (metallic sulfates) or a specific stage in the purification of antimony or mercury, seen as a "devouring" acidic agent.</note> gives off its **vital essence** <note>original: "Gluten"; a sticky, soulful substance believed to be contained within the primary matter.</note> through this heat of the fire / which is called the **Air** / over the **dead head** <note>original Latin: "caput mortuum"; the dregs or useless residue left in the bottom of a flask after distillation.</note> pour its **phlegm** <note>original: "Phlegma"; the watery, tasteless part of a substance that comes over early in distillation.</note> / set it **in dung** <note>original Latin: "in fimo"; a method of gentle heating by burying the vessel in a pile of warm, fermenting horse manure to maintain a constant, low temperature.</note> to putrefy / then distill it as at first / so even more **spirits** come off / drive [the heat] stronger / so a lemon-colored, thick oil goes over the remaining **dead head** / pour back its first distilled water / set to putrefy / then filtered again / and distilled as at first / finally with the strongest heat in an open fire / so a blood-red oil comes over / and that is called the **Fire** / Place the remaining earth in a **reverberatory furnace** <note>A furnace that reflects or "reverberates" heat from the roof onto the material, used here for intense heating.</note> / **calcine** <note>To burn or heat a substance to a high temperature to reduce it to a dry powder.</note> it until it becomes entirely white / then it is ready.

Now take one part of the earth / one part of the **white sulfur** / and two parts of its first water / place in a vial in the **athanor** <note>A self-feeding alchemical furnace designed to maintain a steady, uniform temperature over a long period of time.</note> / so that it incorporates / and **coagulates** / then again pour in one part of its **sulfur** / and two parts of water as before / until you have brought and **fixed** <note>Made a substance stable so that it no longer evaporates or changes when exposed to fire.</note> all the white sulfur / or the **Air** / into the white earth or into its own **ferment** / so you will find a white stone, transparent as crystal / it **tinges** <note>original: "thingiert"; to transform the nature and color of a base metal into a noble one.</note> every metal into the best [silver] / (stable **in the ash-test** <note>original Latin: "in cineritio"; referring to cupellation, a process where metal is heated in a cup of bone ash to test its purity; if it survives, it is "fixed" and true.</note>).

But if you wish, my son, to bring it to the highest perfection / namely to the highest **Redness** / then take the second oil, refined to the highest degree / and pour it over the whitened, shining earth / which should be well-ground on a smooth marble slab / place in a vial / pour the third part of the oil over it / coagulate it in the **athanor** / as was first taught for the white stone / perform this work until you have brought all the oil into it / as you have now dealt with the **Air** / so deal with the **Fire** / with the blood-red oil / refined to the highest degree / so you will make the reddest stone of all / translucent like a ruby / penetrating / flowing / and its nature comparing itself to a true **carbuncle** <note>A legendary deep-red gemstone, often used to describe the finished Philosopher's Stone.</note> and ruby / it **tinges** every metal into the best **Gold** <note>symbol: ☉</note> and the human body to its highest health.

**Thanks be to God.**

# An Augmentation with the Mercury of Saturn.

## THE PROCESS <note>original Latin: *PROCESSVS*</note>

Take six *Loth* <note>A historical German unit of weight, approximately 15 grams or half an ounce.</note> of **Minium of Lead** <note>original: *Saturni Menig*; red lead oxide.</note> and four *Loth* of common salt; grind them both finely together, put them into a large crucible, and place them in the glowing coals until it becomes glowing hot, stirring it constantly with a piece of wood so that it is well **calcined** <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile matter or reduce it to a powder.</note>. Do this two or three times. Afterward, wash away the salt with hot water, and you will find the fine Minium at the bottom; the finer it is, the better.

Take at least four *Loth* of this same Minium, three *Loth* of **sublimated mercury** <note>original: *Mercuriū sublimatum*; corrosive sublimate, a toxic compound used as a reagent.</note>, and two *Loth* of extracted **sal ammoniac** <note>Ammonium chloride; the text notes it must be sublimated again with salt and iron filings.</note>. Grind these pieces together finely and put them into a glass flask. Pour a strong **aqua fortis** <note>original: *Scheydwasser*; literally "parting water," typically nitric acid used to separate metals.</note> over it until it is well covered. Draw it off through an alembic head using a **Mary’s bath** <note>original: *Bal. Mariæ*; a water bath or bain-marie, providing gentle, even heat.</note> until it reaches an oily consistency. Pour the aqua fortis back onto it and draw it off again to an oiliness. Do this a third time.

Afterward, pour a good **spirit of wine** <note>original: *Spiritum vini*; concentrated ethanol or brandy.</note> over it, in which one *Loth* of sal ammoniac has been dissolved and left to stand overnight. Draw the spirit of wine off via the Mary’s bath until nothing more comes over. Pour it back on and draw it off again. On the third time, with the great heat of the Mary’s bath, the entire substance will rise over into the receiver. This may also be **putrefied** <note>A process of slow digestion or fermentation in gentle heat, often lasting weeks.</note> for eight or fourteen days before the final distillation; then distill it over. Pour the distilled material back and distill it over once more so that everything rises. In this way, the entire material has entered into the four elements and is called the **Hellish Borax Water**, which turns **Lead** <note>Symbol: ♄ (Saturn).</note> into a viscous substance.

Now take thinly beaten **Lead** <note>Symbol: ♄</note> and put it into a glass flask. Pour the previously mentioned **Borax Water** over it so that it is well covered. Place it in warm ashes, well-sealed at the top. Let it stand for four hours, and the Borax Water will turn the Lead into a **viscous**

## To fix a mercury into a precipitate.

Take an **oil of vitriol** <note>Concentrated sulfuric acid.</note>, **calcine** mercury in it, and leave it in **digestion** <note>Gentle heating over a long period.</note> for 24 hours. Draw the water off from it, and you have it.

### The Fixing Water is prepared thus.

### Upon the first Water of Copper <note>original: *Veneris*</note>.

## Practice.

Take two parts of the first elemental fire, one part of the Calx of the Sun <note>original: *Kalch Solis*; gold reduced to a fine powder or oxide through heat</note>, and red gold. [Mix with] Alkalis <note>original: *Alcaliers*; alkaline salts used as a flux</note> together through putrefaction <note>original: *per putrefactionem*; the alchemical stage of decomposition through gentle warmth</note> for forty days; the Ferment of Gold thus:

Dissolve gold in its water <note>likely *aqua regia*, a powerful acid capable of dissolving gold</note>, let it evaporate until it reaches an oily consistency <note>original: *Olitet*</note>, then pour fresh water upon it and draw it off; for the fifth time, set it to putrefaction for its allotted time, until you see at the beginning of its tincture that the bottom is white. Reduce it into a body <note>To bring the substance back into a solid, metallic state</note>. You shall graduate <note>refine or increase the potency of</note> this Tincture of the Sun beyond 24 or 28, up to 34 degrees.

Take half a part of this Red Lion <note>A symbolic term for a potent alchemical substance, often associated with purified iron or antimony</note> and three times as much of his sister’s Sulfur <note>original: *Sulphuris*; refers to the "soul" or combustible principle of a metal</note>, which is the other part; that is the incombustible Fire of Mercury. Coagulate it in its Lion, in its glass, with the Number 3.

## The Practice.

Take the <term>body of Jupiter</term> <note>original: *corpus Iovis*; the alchemical name for the metal tin</note>; calcine it and reverberate <note>to heat a substance in a furnace so that the flames are turned back onto it</note> it into a subtle <term>alkali</term> <note>original: *Alculi*; likely referring to a salt or alkaline ash</note>. Dissolve it in its own water, and let it putrefy <note>undergo chemical decomposition through gentle warmth</note> for a philosophical month <note>traditionally 40 days</note>. Separate the elements: the element of fire will be gold-colored. Rectify <note>purify through repeated distillation</note> this fire through its matching retort.

Of this fire of Jupiter, take one part; of the sulfur of the Sun <note>Gold</note>, half a part; and of its own <term>living water of mercury</term> <note>original: *aquam viuam Mercurij*; likely a distilled mercurial solvent</note>, three times as much by weight as the previous substances. Coagulate all of this by weight together into a stone in a "Number 3" glass.

One part of this prepared <term>Tincture of Jupiter</term> <note>original: *Tinctur Iouis*</note> added to 100 parts of mercury <note>symbol: ☿</note> will become a yellow precipitate. One part of this <term>precipitate</term> <note>a solid substance that settles out of a liquid solution</note> added to 300 parts of the <term>body of Jupiter</term> <note>tin</note> will tinge <note>alchemically transform</note> it into good <term>gold</term> <note>original: *Sol*</note>. However, it will be lighter in weight; restore this balance with its own gold <note>symbol: ☉</note>.

## Upon the Saturn of Copper.

<note>original: *Saturnum Venereis*; This heading refers to a process involving both lead (Saturn) and copper (Venus).</note>

Command and order <term>Saturn</term> <note>lead</note> to become a <term>Venus</term> <note>copper</note>. Turn this copper into a <term>vitriol</term> <note>a sulfate of a metal, often appearing as glassy crystals</note>, and dissolve this vitriol into an oil.

Take Saturn, calcine it, and then dissolve it in an alum water. Draw it off until it reaches an oily consistency <note>original: *Olitet*</note>; keep this as one part. Take a good yellow sulfur made from copper ore and sublimate it with <term>calcined vitriol</term> <note>original: *Vitriolo calcinato*; vitriol that has been heated to a dry powder</note> several times so that it purifies itself well and gives off—or becomes—beautiful white flowers <note>original: *Flores*; the fine powder produced by sublimation</note>.

Reverberate these to a red-brown color, dissolve them with vinegar, and then dissolve them into an oil. Separate the vinegar from it and keep that oil.

# The process follows as an example /
## and is an augmentation.

Take four <term>lots</term><note>A historical unit of weight, roughly 15 grams or half an ounce.</note> of <term>Luna</term><note>The alchemical name for silver.</note>; dissolve it in common <term>parting water</term><note>original: "Scheydwasser"; nitric acid, used to separate silver from gold.</note>; draw it off in a <term>circulatory vessel</term><note>original: "Zirckreibs"; a glass vessel used for distillation where the vapors condense and flow back down.</note> and pour it back over it; draw it off again until the <term>spirits</term><note>The volatile acidic vapors of the acid.</note> come over; pour it back over again; repeat this pouring on and drawing off seven times, then the <term>Oil of Luna</term><note>A concentrated, liquid state of silver achieved through repeated distillation with acid.</note> is prepared. Take this Oil of Luna, put it into a small flask, and set it to <term>coagulate</term><note>The process of thickening or solidifying a liquid.</note>; and give it a fine, gentle fire and <term>fix</term><note>The process of making a substance stable in heat so it no longer evaporates.</note> it until it becomes fixed; test this on a copper plate: when it no longer smokes, it is ready; but if it still smokes, fix it even longer. Add more Oil of Luna to this <term>fire-stone</term><note>original: "Firenstein"; the fixed solid residue resulting from the process.</note> and fix it again; you may make as much of this fire-stone as you wish; thus you can <term>augment</term><note>To increase the quantity or potency of the alchemical substance.</note> it without end, and make as much as you desire.

When you now have a good amount of the fire-stone, take as much of it as you like, and let it flow into <term>Gold</term><note>original: "Goldt"; the fire-stone is added to molten gold to increase its volume or quality.</note>; and introduce this fire-stone into it with a quick <term>flux</term><note>The state of the metal being molten and flowing.</note>, and precipitate it through <term>antimony</term><note>A metallic element used in the crucible to purify gold from other metals.</note>; and if it were not high enough in <term>color</term><note>Alchemists judged the purity and "soul" of gold by the richness of its yellow hue.</note>, give it the color through the <term>Royal Cement</term><note>original: "Ziment Regal"; a refining process using salts and heat to remove impurities from gold.</note>; in this work, the onset of <term>fixity</term><note>original: "Firigkeit"; the quality of being stable and resistant to fire.</note> must be waited for. # A secret Suginol-process, or how to introduce six loth of gold into a mark of silver.

Take Suginol <term>mercury</term><note>symbol: ☿</note> made and boiled with <term>vitriol</term><note>original: "V.V."; likely Vitriolum Venus (copper vitriol) or common vitriol used as a corrosive agent.</note> as vagabonds are accustomed to making it; five <term>loth</term><note>A historical unit of weight, roughly 15-17 grams.</note> of fine white <term>jasee</term><note>An alchemical term for a specific mineral or salt, possibly a type of white arsenic or gypsum.</note>, and four loth of <term>tartar</term><note>Potassium bitartrate, a salty crust found in wine barrels, used here as a chemical flux.</note> called Giniton. Crush these three things together into a fine powder; this is the cleansing powder.

Take two loth of fine silver from the parting <note>The process of separating silver from gold.</note> or from another source where no gold is present, and melt it into a bead. Place six loth of the aforementioned cleansing powder into a clean <term>crucible</term><note>original: "Digel"; a heat-resistant ceramic container used for melting metals.</note>, well-packed, and place the silver bead in the center. Seal the crucible well and set it in a wind furnace for three hours with a gentle fire, so that the glowing coals just cover it. Afterward, heat it for two full hours with a strong fire until it melts. Then take fresh cleansing powder as before, and let the <term>body</term><note>original: "corpus"; refers to the physical mass of the metal.</note> react within it for five hours, so that the <term>nigredo</term><note>original: "Nigredo"; the "blackness," which alchemists believed represented the state of impurity or symbolic death of the metal before it could be purified.</note> is mostly removed.

Take this cleansed body just as it has come out of the fire, file it small, and roughly powder it with common <term>chybural</term><note>An alchemical term usually referring to a form of sulfur or a mineral salt used for reacting with metals.</note>, estimating by eye so that it can be pounded into a powder. Rub three loth of Suginol into this; once well-rubbed, put it into a single-neck flask. Pour enough of the "following water" <note>The specific recipe for this "water" likely appeared on a previous page or was common knowledge to the practitioner.</note> over it so that it is well-covered. Let it <term>coagulate</term><note>To thicken or solidify a liquid into a solid mass through gentle heat.</note> in a sand bath with gentle heat until completely dry. Then pour fresh water over it again as mentioned, and let it dry out once more. Do this with the fresh water four times or more. Then let it <term>fix</term><note>original: "figiren"; the process of making a substance stable and non-volatile so it no longer evaporates when heated.</note> with strong heat, buried deep in the sand without water for four days and nights; thus it becomes a <term>precipitate</term><note>A solid substance that has settled out of a solution or changed state through chemical reaction.</note>.

Now take this precipitate and place it in a clean crucible, well-packed and only covered at the top. Set the crucible in a circular fire or bed of embers so that the coals touch it, though not with a strong fire. In this way, the sharp <term>spirits</term><note>Volatile acidic vapors or gases released during the heating process.</note> will gradually <term>evaporate</term><note>original: "efumieren".</note> away. Let this happen for two hours with a gentle fire, or longer, until it is seen that the spirits are gone. Then, let it glow well for half an hour...

# Process of a secret Graduating Water/
## in which silver is graduated to the Rhenish standard/ by a short method.

In waters in which <term>Poad: an alchemical code name for gold</term>, that is, <term>gold: symbolized by ☉</term> <note>original: "☉"</note> is resolved into a spirit, there lies a great secret. Although it may consume <note>original: "zentzughet," likely meaning to withdraw or dissolve away</note> the metal, it accomplishes everything through its ability to penetrate the silver and bring it to a high grade, in which nothing is lost. While there is a short way to dissolve the gold into a viscous state <note>original: "ad viſcoſam"</note>, it is not to be revealed, especially to frivolous or haughty people.

And here follows a Parasolon <note>a "shield" or specific instructional step</note>, that is, a procedure by which the gold is brought into a viscous state. Take three <term>Loth: a unit of weight, roughly 15 grams</term> of gold, hammered into thin sheets; put it with three <term>Quintlin: a small weight, 1/4 of a Loth</term> of Albacheton Rubei, which is <term>cinnabar: a bright red mineral also known as mercury sulfide</term> <note>original: "Zinober"</note>, into a <term>cementing box: a crucible used for the dry refinement of metals</term>. Let it <term>macerate: soak or soften</term> in very hot sand for two hours. Grind it fine for half an hour. Afterward, grind into it three Loth of Volucum Fantasson <note>compare to "Volucum Santallon" on the previous page</note>, which is <term>mercury sublimate: a highly toxic compound of mercury and chlorine</term> <note>original: "☿ ſublimatum"</note>, acting as a "key." Put it into a <term>luted: sealed with airtight clay or paste</term> vial. Let it rise and descend <note>a cycle of evaporation and condensation</note> in the hot sand from the gold thirty times, until the gold becomes viscous. Take this together with the mercury sublimate that has risen, and grind it all fine together. Put it into a <term>flask: a glass vessel with a long neck</term> <note>original: "Kolbenglaß"</note> and pour a strong <term>Jasoron: an alchemical code word for a potent solvent or acid</term> over it, so that it stands a finger's breadth high above it. Draw it up <note>distill it</note> in the sand and bring it to an <term>oily state: a thick, concentrated consistency</term> <note>original: "Olitet"</note>. Do this strongly for a third time, and a <term>precipitate: a solid substance that settles out of a liquid</term> will remain. Take this and grind it fine; put it into a glass. Take three Loth of the following <term>flux: a substance used to promote melting</term>, well-weighed; dissolve it in half a measure of vinegar. Pour all of this onto the precipitate and let it cook down gently until it is completely dry, stirring it constantly. Afterward, take the precipitate and three Loth of fine silver that has been purified by <term>white sulfur: likely refers to a specific refining process using sulfur</term> <note>original: "Sulphur album"</note> and granulated into small grains. Arrange them <term>layer upon layer</term> <note>original: "ſtratum ſuper ſtratum"</note> in a clean crucible. Cover this and let it heat up gently in a <term>wind furnace: a furnace that uses a natural or forced draft of air to reach high temperatures</term>, and finally heat it strongly for half an hour. Thus you will find the fine silver converted into gold of the <term>Rhenish standard: the high purity level required for the Rhenish guilder currency</term>.

# Tincturing Grading Oil of the Black Eagle

...let it cool, and you will find a red-brown stone. Grind this small and take the flux described below, weighing exactly as much as the <term>precipitate: the solid substance that settles out of a liquid solution</term>. Having ground them together and placed them in a crucible, first let it melt gently, and then strongly in a <term>wind furnace: a high-heat furnace that uses a natural or forced draft of air</term>. This will cause a <term>regulus: a button of pure metal found at the bottom of a crucible, historically called a "king"</term> to settle. Refine this button on the <term>cupel: a porous ceramic bowl used to separate precious metals from base metals through high heat</term>. From the Mercury, you will immediately be left with 18 <term>loth: a historical weight, roughly half an ounce or 15-16 grams</term> of good gold, which will remain stable in all tests. I say, however, that a short <term>fixation: the process of making a volatile substance stable enough to withstand fire</term> achieves nothing here.

### The Flux

Take a half-<term>vierling: a quarter-pound measure</term> of raw <term>tartar: a salty crust found in wine barrels, used as a purifying agent</term>, one vierling of common salt, three vierlings of <term>litharge: lead monoxide, used here to help the metals flow and separate</term>, and one loth of iron filings. Grind everything together finely. Boil it four times gently in <term>brine: salt water</term>, drying it thoroughly each time. Then the flux is ready.

### Process with the Silver, and 10 Loth of good Silver remains from the Mercury, in which the fourth part is Gold.

-> Amalgam <-

Take a half-pound of running mercury and place it in an iron pan. Take two <term>maß: a historical liquid measure, roughly 1 to 1.5 liters</term> of running water and dissolve within it four loth of <term>verdigris: the green pigment or crust formed on copper</term> <note>original: "Acustum"</note>, one and a half loth of yellow sulfur, and six loth of common salt. Grind everything small and pour enough of this water over the mercury so that it is well covered. Boil it, constantly pouring more water on, and continue boiling for five hours. Afterward, take the mercury and let it harden in the air.

# Tincturing Grading of the Black Eagle

Now take 15 <term>loth: a historical weight, roughly 15-16 grams</term> of this coagulated <term>Mercury: quicksilver</term>, and the same amount of purified <term>Luna: silver</term>, two loth of the extracted redness from <term>vitriol: a sulfate mineral</term> as described in the previous section, and one and a half loth of <term>cinnabar: a bright red mercury ore</term>. Grind all these pieces together finely for a good hour. Place them in a flask that is somewhat flat on the bottom and pour the previously mentioned vitriol oil over it until it is well-moistened. <term>Lute: seal the vessel with an airtight paste</term> the glass and place it in warm sand—at a heat where you can barely stand to keep your hand in it—for a day and a night. On the second night, increase the heat. On the third, heat it until everything glows. Then take the material out and <term>reduce: restore a chemical substance to its metallic form</term> it with the previously mentioned flux. First melt it strongly, then refine it through <note>original: "per ♄"</note> <term>lead: symbolized by Saturn (♄)</term> on a cupel. Immediately, from the Mercury, you will be left with 10 loth of Silver, containing four parts of <term>Sol: gold</term>.

### Tincturing Cementing Powder, as worked by a Count of Görlitz.

<image-desc>A single decorative symbol resembling a hash mark or gridded bar.</image-desc>

Take the upper coagulated substance, the extracted vitriol (or *Stemo* <note>likely stibnite, the primary ore of antimony</note>), and cinnabar. Grind these three pieces very finely for one hour and place them in a glass. Pour the vitriol oil over them. Set the sealed glass in sand and let it work for two days and nights. After that, heat it more strongly for three days, and then for two more days until the glass glows through; in this way, the material will be <term>fixed: rendered stable and resistant to evaporation by fire</term>. Grind this small, return it to a glass, moisten it again with the vitriol oil, and let it boil down for two days and nights. Then the powder is ready.

Now take at least two parts of fine silver and file it small. Into this, grind nine <term>quintle: a small unit of weight, approximately 3.6 grams</term> of the prepared fixed powder. Place it into an earthenware <term>cementation box: a specialized container used to heat-treat metals in a bed of reactive powder</term> and set it in sand for 30 hours: 10 hours with a gentle fire, 10 hours somewhat stronger, and for the final 10 hours, keep the box covered with sand and a charcoal fire built on top. Then let it cool. Grind the previously mentioned flux into it and reduce it to a <term>regulus: a button of metallic "king" found at the bottom of a crucible</term>. Refine this, and you will have the "yellow needle," and the Silver is fixed; this is for high <term>grading: the process of refining or improving the quality and color of a metal</term>. Here end the Colophonian pieces. The "Black Eagle" is <term>antimony: a metallic element used to purify gold</term>, which contains elevated Gold within itself.

# A Particular Work which a
## poor journeyman should work.

In the beginning, when I started to work [alchemically], I supported myself for a long time with the following little piece <note>The author uses "Stücklein" (little piece) to refer to a specific alchemical recipe or process.</note>. When I obtained a better one, I gave this little piece to my brother Onophero in the year 1414; he did not think much of alchemy, but when he saw the truth for himself and worked it, he would have gladly devoured the art out of love for it. Although true <term>particularia: alchemical processes that transform only a specific amount or type of metal, rather than a universal elixir</term> are rare enough, it occasionally happens that to whom God grants it, and upon whom He gives His rich blessing, [the work succeeds]; the eternal justice of God also wishes to be petitioned for one's livelihood.

<image-desc>A decorative crosshatch or grid-like symbol with three vertical lines and two horizontal lines.</image-desc>

<margin>†</margin>
### Process.

Take three <term>loth: a historical unit of weight, approximately 15-16 grams</term> of good <term>steno: likely stibnite, the primary ore of antimony</term>, two loth of finely filed good steel, and one loth of finely filed <term>Venus: copper</term>. Crush these pieces and grind them well together; put everything on a <term>cupel: a shallow, porous ceramic dish used in refining</term> and let the *steno* smoke very strongly away from it until no more *steno* is perceived. Then take fresh <term>antimony</term>, grind three loth again into these two metals, and let the *steno* smoke away once more. Do this for a third time with fresh *steno*, and you will find the two metals prepared. Grind these very small and add an equal weight of <term>impasted mercury: quicksilver that has been made into a paste or amalgam</term>; add common <term>mountain sulfur</term> (which is called <term>cinnabar</term> <note>original: "Zinober"</note> at this time) to it. Put it all together into a <term>luted crucible: a melting pot sealed with an airtight paste</term> and place it for three hours in hot sand until the mercury has <term>cemented: a process of heating a metal in a powder to alter its properties</term> away. Then the two metals have <term>ingress: the power of an alchemical substance to penetrate and transform a metal</term> into <term>Luna: silver</term>.

# A particular work that a poor journeyman should perform.

Take one <term>loth: a unit of weight, approximately 15 grams</term> of fine silver, white mountain-feather <note>original: "Bergkfeder"; likely asbestos or a fibrous alum</note>, and common salt, half a loth of each well-weighed. Let the silver flow entirely therein for one strong hour; then let it flow again on its own so that it purifies itself; then it is ready.

Now take one <term>quintle: a small unit of weight, about 3.75 grams</term> of the prepared metal ground small in a paper with a little grain of borax. Let the loth of silver that was prepared flow strongly by itself and throw [the powder] upon it. Let them go together for a quarter of an hour. Afterward, refine it by way of <term>Saturn: alchemical code for lead, referring here to cupellation</term>; thus you have **fixed silver** <note>original: "Lunam fixam"; silver that has been "fixed" to resist chemical change or heat</note>. Up to this point, I have taught it to my brother. I tell you, if the purified silver appears like a yellow needle on the half-mark, then take one loth of gold; add it to that same silver and let it flow. Cast one quintle of the prepared metal upon it and let it go for a quarter of an hour. Cast another quintle upon it, and everything remains the best **Gold** <note>The symbol ☉ is used in the original for Gold</note>. Only see to it that the stone flows strongly on the cupel with the metal, so that the cinnabar can thereafter take hold of the metal.

Rub these pieces together very small; put them into an earthenware vessel. Pour a fortified urine <note>original: "gefütterten Vrin"; likely urine that has been aged or concentrated</note> upon it until moistened, and let this become dry and ground. Do this six times, and then the powder is ready.

Take one loth of this powder and put it into a glass flask; pour two loth of <term>Iasoron: a cryptic alchemical term, likely referring to a specific corrosive solvent or mineral water</term> upon it, in which eight loth of silver should be dissolved, along with a sixteenth part of the first prepared <term>Mars: iron</term> with <term>Venus: copper</term>. Precipitate it in a sand bath until it becomes a stone. Let it stand for four days and nights in hot sand, so that whatever is volatile sublimates upward. Then take the material in the glass and put it into a crucible. Let it flow very strongly by itself in a covered wind-furnace. Thus a **king** <note>original: "König" (regulus); a button of pure metal found at the bottom of the crucible after smelting</note> settles, and whatever of the slag is there, carry that into a...

### Another work follows.

Take a quarter-measure of <term>Stemo: a historical term for antimony</term> and half a pound of common running <term>Mercury: quicksilver</term>; make a paste in the antimony and sublimate it from there, so that the mercury rises upon this sublimated mercury. ### Finally, remember me.

<margin>Antimony</margin>

Two incombustible, eternal lights are found herein, which I, Bartholomeus Korndorffer, have transcribed from a disciple of Lord Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim. He <note>the disciple</note> assured me by his oath that they have never yet come to the light of day, for the Abbot only gifted the secret of his heart to a single great <term>potentate: a powerful monarch or ruler</term>. This highly renowned <term>Magus: a master of hidden or natural wisdom</term> <note>original: "Magus"</note> Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, who lived during the time of the great Emperor Maximilian I, never found his equal in Germany in those days. He performed and established much good through his arts, and none of it was mixed with devilish works, as some wicked people have falsely accused and charged him. Rather, it came from the <term>constellation of secrets: likely referring to the intersection of astrology and hidden natural laws</term> <note>original German: "Gestirn der heymligkeit"</note>, through which he learned everything that happened in the world whenever he wished. He also many times foretold things to come. Once, when I was on my travels, I came to St. Moritz and unexpectedly found an acquaintance from the Elector’s courts. I spoke with him, and he was glad to see me; he invited me to dine with him, saying he wished to invite another to join us, named Servatius Hochel. This man had been with the Abbot of Sponheim and had served him for about twelve years. I was quite pleased with this. My acquaintance informed me that Hochel was a reserved and quiet man, though occasionally he would let slip a <term>hint: literally a 'snap' or a small, sudden insight</term> <note>original: "Schnall"</note> regarding the arts. When we had gathered and finished the meal, Mr. Hochel asked me to go with him to his lodgings—

### Here follows the process and the practice.

Take eight <term>loth: a historical German unit of weight, approximately 15 grams or half an ounce</term> of sulfur, and an equal amount of calcined alum. Rub these two pieces together. Let the sulfur rise through the alum; within eight hours, it is prepared.

Of this <note>referring to the matter described at the end of the previous process</note>, take at least five <term>Loth: a historical German unit of weight, approximately 1/2 ounce or 15 grams</term>, and two loth of good crystalline Venetian <term>Borax: a mineral salt used as a flux in alchemy and metalworking</term>. # Preface.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'A' at the beginning of the text, featuring ornate floral scrollwork and leaf patterns within a square border.</image-desc>

Aphidius <note>An alchemical authority frequently cited in medieval texts, though his historical identity is obscure.</note>, one of the ancient sages, says that for one who cannot imagine anything for himself in the Art <note>In this context, "the Art" refers to the Great Work of alchemy.</note> of the **Philosopher’s Stone**, it is more useful that he does not engage with it at all than that he attempts something. Rasis <note>The Latinized name of Abū Bakr al-Rāzī (c. 865–925), a Persian polymath and one of the most important figures in the history of medicine and alchemy.</note> speaks similarly in the book *Lumen Luminum* <note>original: "Lumen Luminum," meaning "Light of Lights." This was a highly influential alchemical text attributed to Rasis.</note>: one must take diligent care—and I also most strongly warn you here—that no one should presume to undertake the unknown mixing of the **Elements**. And Rosinus <note>A Latinized name for Zosimos of Panopolis, a Greek-Egyptian alchemist from the 3rd or 4th century.</note> also intends this, saying: all those who involve themselves in this Art and lack the understanding and knowledge of the things which the Philosophers have written in their books, they are without understanding. For the philosophers have established the foundation of this art in a natural beginning, but one of hidden operation. Although it is evident that all physical things take their origin from the Earth, and likewise their essence, according to the order of time, they are brought forth by the influence of the stars or **Planets**—such as the **Sun** and **Moon** and the others—together with the four **Qualities** <note>In Aristotelian physics, these are the four primary properties: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note> of the elements, which move them without ceasing. Through this, all and every growing and procreating thing is produced, each according to its own particular kind.

<summary>The author opens the preface by citing classical alchemical authorities to warn the uninitiated against practicing alchemy without proper theoretical understanding. It establishes that the "Art" is based on natural principles, planetary influences, and the four qualities of the elements.</summary>

# Splendor Solis.

...[the matter] <note>The text continues from the previous page's discussion on heat acting upon the matter.</note> not the [process of] the Philosophers, but their **putrefaction** <term>putrefaction: the decomposition or "death" of the base matter, considered the essential first stage of the alchemical Great Work</term> is a moistening or an imbuing, through which dry things reach their fiery state, so that they may become green and grow. In putrefaction, moisture is united with dryness and not destroyed, so that the moist part holds the dry parts together; and this is properly called a **trituration** <term>trituration: the reduction of a substance to a fine powder through grinding or rubbing</term>. However, if the moisture is entirely separated from the dryness, it becomes necessary to boil down the dry parts and transform them into ashes.

This **incernation** <term>incernation: an alchemical term for "making into flesh," or giving a physical, bodily form to a spiritual substance</term> is not what the Philosophers desire; rather, they intend for their putrefaction, imbuing, trituration, and **calcination** <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to remove volatile substances or to oxidize it into a powder</term> to occur in such a way that the natural moisture and dryness are purified together, separated from superfluous moisture, and dried, once the corruptible parts have been extracted. 

This is just as food that enters the **belly of the intestines** <note>original: "Thicini Bauch", likely a corruption of the Latin "intestini," referring to the digestive tract.</note> is cooked and broken down, and the nourishing power and moisture are drawn from it—whereby Nature is sustained and increased—and its superfluous parts are cast off. # SECOND TREATISE.

Morienus <note>original: "Moriens"; referring to Morienus Romanus, a legendary 12th-century alchemist</note> says: You should know that the entire work of this Art concludes in two skills <note>original: "geschicklichkeiten" — meaning operations or processes</note> that are so linked together that when one is accomplished, the other begins and completes the work. Then the entire mastery is perfect; however, these do not occur except within their own matter. To understand this properly, one must first know what Nature, as the giver, says in its Mercury <note>original: "Mercurij"</note> regarding the creation of metals: she produces metals from Mercury and Sulfur. This is also what Ferrarius <note>Likely Efferarius Monachus, a 13th-century alchemical writer</note> intends in his *Inquiry into Alchemy* <note>original: "Frag von der Alchimia"</note> in the 25th chapter.
<margin>x</margin> That Nature, from the very beginning of the natural metals, takes in the fire a slimy, heavy water, mixed with a very white, agile, and heavy earth. She resolves this into a vapor <note>original: "Prodem" — an archaic term for an exhalation or steam</note> or steam, and raises it into the veins or crevices of the earth. There she cooks or steams them together, constantly [removing] the moisture and thus drying them as they unite, until a substance is formed that is called <term>Quicksilver</term> <note>mercury</note>. This is now the beginning and the very first matter of the metals, as was also mentioned above. Therefore, he speaks again in the 26th chapter, saying: those who wish to follow Nature should not take Quicksilver alone, but Quicksilver and Sulfur joined together—not common quicksilver and sulfur, but that which Nature has joined together, well-prepared and cooked in constant fluidity. In such a quicksilver, Nature has begun with her first effect and ended in a metallic nature, and there she has stopped. For she has accomplished her part and left everything to the Art <note>meaning the alchemist's skill</note> to complete the same into a perfect <term>Philosophers' Stone</term>. In these words, it is made known to everyone that whoever wishes to proceed correctly in this Art—as all the philosophers say—should begin where Nature has left off, and should take the sulfur and the quicksilver which Nature has joined together in the most pure form.

# Now follows the way through which the entire Work of this <term>Art or Mastery</term><note>The "Art" or "Mastery" refers to Alchemy, specifically the creation of the Philosopher's Stone.</note> concludes, and it is demonstrated through several Parables, Figures, Discourses, and the diverse sayings of the <term>Philosophers of Philosophers</term><note>original: "Philosophi Philosophorum"; refers to the highest authorities in the alchemical tradition, such as Hermes, Aristotle, and Avicenna.</note>.

## THE THIRD TREATISE.

<note>original: "Hermes ein Vatter der Philosophen"</note>Hermes, a Father of the Philosophers, says: "It is yet to be that an end of this world, heaven, and earth come together." No one can [easily master] the two aforementioned skills through heaven and earth, for many accidents arise in the work before it is brought to an end and understood through the allegories of the figures, as follows hereafter. And this is the First Parable:

God created the Earth in the beginning, simple, flat, and very fertile, without spirit, and without sand, stone, mountain, or valley. Through the influence of the planets and the workings of Nature, the Earth has now been transformed into many forms: outwardly with hard stones, high mountains, and deep valleys; and inwardly with strange things and colors, namely the ores and their origins. With such things, the Earth has completely departed from its first form. 

This resulted from such things initially: for although the Earth was heaped up thick, large, deep, long, wide, and broad, yet through the constant effect of the sun's heat, there arose within it a sweltering, hot, vaporous, and steamy warmth. This warmth permeated the entire Earth to its very abyss and produced—within the coldness and moisture of the Earth—a strong vapor, both misty and airy. All of these were enclosed within the Earth, and after a long time, they increased so much and at last became so strong that the Earth could no longer <meta>catchword: contain</meta> [them...]

<summary>This page introduces the third treatise of the Splendor Solis, moving from theory to parables that describe the alchemical process. It begins with a geological metaphor, explaining how planetary influence and internal heat transform the primordial, flat Earth into a complex world of mountains and minerals.</summary>

contained; because they naturally desired to rise upwards, and finally at the ends of the Earth, where many were gathered together, they heaped a portion of the earth in one place, and another there, creating many a hill, mountain, and deep valley. And in those places where such hills and mountains came to be, there the Earth was most excellently cooked, boiled, and blended with Heat, Cold, Moisture, and Dryness. And it is there that the best <term>ore</term><note>original: "Erz"; refers to the unrefined metallic minerals found in the earth, which alchemists believed grew like plants.</note> is found. But where the Earth is flat, they heaped nothing, and for that reason such vapors and smoke are not found there. Furthermore, where the outer Earth was especially slimy, clay-like, and <term>fatty</term><note>original: "feyst"; in alchemical terms, "fatness" or "oiliness" refers to the presence of the sulfurous principle, which was thought to be the "fuel" of metallic growth.</note>, moisture pressed down from above, through which it became soft again and settled into a firm, dough-like consistency. Through the drying of the sun's heat and the passage of time, it was increasingly firmed, hardened, and baked. 

However, the Earth which is brittle and crumbly, like small grit and sand, and has little substance, clings together like grapes; that same Earth is too lean and sparse in its fatness and had too little moisture. Therefore, it is not sufficiently baked together and remains clumpy, like a thick porridge that has not been stirred, or like a mealy dough that has been given too little water. For no Earth can become stone unless it is made from fatty sliminess or slimy Earth, well-drenched and mixed with moisture; for after the sun's heat has drawn out the water, the moisture of the Earth must hold it together, otherwise it remains crumbly and brittle and falls apart again. 

That which has not yet become perfectly hard may even today, through the constant workings of Nature and the sun’s heat, become hard and firm stone. ## The Second Parable.

Hermes, the first Master of this Art, speaks thus: the water of the air, which exists between Heaven and Earth, is the life of every thing; for through its moisture and warmth, this is the medium between the two opposites, such as Fire and Water. And that same water has rained down upon the Earth; the Heavens have opened up and dewed upon the Earth, whereby she has become sweet, like honey, and moistened. That same blood brings forth many kinds of colors and fruits, and in their midst has grown a great tree with a silver trunk, which spreads itself to the corners of the world. Upon its branches sat many kinds of birds, which all flew away toward the day, and the **Raven’s Head**<note>original: "Rappen Haupt"; in alchemy, the "Raven's Head" or *Caput Corvi* symbolizes the *nigredo* (blackness) stage, the initial state of putrefaction that must be overcome.</note> has become white. The same tree brings manifold fruits: the first are the very finest pearls; the second is called by the Philosophers <term>foliated earth</term><note>original: "Terra foliata"; this refers to the "White Earth," a purified state of the alchemical matter that has been cleansed of impurities.</note>; the third is the very finest Gold. This tree also gives fruits of health; it makes warm what is cold, and what is warm it makes cold; it makes the dry moist, and the moist dry; it makes the hard soft, and the soft hard; and this is the end of the whole Art. Of this speaks the Author of the Three Words<note>Referring to the alchemist Senior Zadith (Ibn Umail) and his text *De Chemia*, which discusses the "Three Words" or principles of the work.</note>: the three moist stones, three precious words of the whole mastery. This is also what Salienus means when he speaks of the herb <term>Lunatica</term><note>original: "Lunatica"; a legendary alchemical plant, also known as Moonwort, believed to follow the lunar cycle and possess the power to transmute metals into silver.</note> or Bera: its root is a metallic earth, it has a red stem, covered or essentially spotted with a blackness that peels off easily. It gains or receives flowers in time; after three days, if one places it in <term>mercury</term><note>original: "Mercurium"; not common quicksilver, but the "Philosophic Mercury" or universal solvent.</note>, it changes into a perfect silver; and if one treats it further, it turns into gold; and this same gold converts a hundred parts into the very finest gold. Virgil mentions this tree in the sixth book of the *Aeneid* when he speaks in his fable of how Aeneas and Silvius went to a tree, and another grew in that same place<note>A reference to the "Golden Bough" in Virgil’s epic, which served as a protective talisman for Aeneas and regenerated immediately when plucked.</note>.

<summary>This page presents the 'Second Parable,' using the allegory of a Silver Tree and the 'Moon-herb' to describe the transformative process of alchemy and the creation of silver and gold. It cites classical and hermetic authorities like Hermes, Virgil, and the Author of the Three Words to validate these mystical processes.</summary>

## The Third Parable.

Avicenna <note>A famous Persian polymath (Ibn Sina) often cited in alchemical texts as a primary authority on the nature of matter.</note> says in the chapter on Moisture: whenever heat acts upon a moist body, it first produces a **Blackness**. For this reason, the ancients saw a mist rising from afar that covered and moistened the whole earth; and they also saw the turbulence of the sea and the flowing waters over the face of the earth, and these became foul and stinking in the darkness. They also saw the King of the Earth <term>King of the Earth: a symbol for the "prime matter" or the base metallic state needing transformation</term> sink down and heard him cry out with an eager voice: "Whoever redeems me shall live with me forever and rule in my clarity upon my royal throne."

And the night surrounded all things. On the following day, they saw a bright Morning Star rise over the King, and the light of day illuminating the darkness. They saw the clear Sun through the clouds in many forms of colors, with its stars and shining rays, and a fragrant scent, surpassing all musk <note>original: "Bisem"; musk was a common alchemical metaphor for the pleasant odor released when a chemical process reached a state of purity</note>, rising from the earth and shining beautifully and clearly.

And in this, everything was perfected, so that the King of all honors was delighted and renewed, well-adorned and quite beautiful; Sun and Moon marveled at his beauty. He was crowned with three precious crowns: one of iron, the second of silver, and the third of gold. They saw in his right hand a sphere <note>original: "Corper"; likely a globus cruciger or symbolic orb</note> containing seven stars, all giving off a glowing brilliance, and in his left hand a golden apple, and upon it sat a white dove of a fiery nature, silvered over, with wings of gold color. 

Regarding this, Aristotle <note>original: "Arles," a common shorthand/corruption for Aristoteles</note> said: "The destruction of one thing is the birth of another." This refers to the masterly Art <term>The Art: Alchemy (the Great Work)</term> and the preparation of the destructive moistures, being renewed in its essential moisture, which is its perfection and life

## The Third Parable.

## The Fifth Parable.

The philosophers assign two bodies to this Art, namely the Sun and the Moon, which are the Earth and the Water; they also call them Man and Woman, and they give birth to four children: two males, which are Heat and Cold, and two females, which are Moisture and Dryness. These are the four elements, and they create the <term>Fifth Essence<note>original: "Fünffte wesen" – also known as the Quintessence, the pure, spiritual core of matter that remains when the four physical elements are balanced.</note></term>, which is the <term>white Magnesia<note>original: "weisse Magnesia" – In alchemy, this refers to a specific mineral substance or a state of matter representing the pure "body" of the Stone before it is colored red.</note></term> that is not false; <term>Senior<note>original: "Senior" — a reference to the 10th-century Arabian alchemist Zadith ben Hamuel, whose "Tabula Chimica" was highly influential.</note></term> concludes this by saying: when these five are gathered together, they will be one thing, from which the Natural Stone is made. <term>Avicenna<note>A famous Persian physician and philosopher; alchemical texts were often attributed to him in the medieval and Renaissance periods.</note></term> says: if we can arrive at the Fifth, then the end of our purpose has come.

In the middle of the yolk is the Fifth, from which the young chick comes and grows; thus in an egg are all the powers along with the matter from which the perfect nature

->THE FOURTH TREATISE<-
<note>original: "TRACTATVS QVARTVS"</note>

Ali <note>original: "Ales"; likely referring to Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arab astrologer and alchemist whose "Book of the Birth of Natural Things" was a common reference.</note> speaks thus in the *Book of Birth*: the seed and the human give birth to a human, for the power and spirit of the seed bring life, and this happens in a sevenfold manner, through the effect of the Sun’s heat. However, since the <term>Philosophers</term> <note>a term for alchemists who seek the underlying truths of nature</note> in their work must assist Nature with <term>Art</term> <note>original: "Kunst"; the skilled practice of alchemy</note>, they must regulate a heat through art, in accordance with the Sun, so that they may give birth to the aforementioned <term>Stone</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the alchemical process</note>; and this also occurs in a sevenfold manner.

Firstly, such a heat is required that softens and melts the thickness of the earth, which has been baked together thick and hard; concerning this, Socrates says: the holes and cracks of the parts of the earth are opened, so that it may take into itself the power of the fire and water.

## THE FIFTH TREATISE <note>original Latin: "TRACTATVS QVINTVS"</note>

### The first Article.

The first thing that is required in the Art of Alchemy <note>original Latin: "Alchimiæ"</note> is the **dissolution**; for the order of Nature requires that the body be cooked in a water—that is, in a quicksilver—and simply put, the "living silver" <term>Living silver: "Argentum vivum" or mercury, considered by alchemists to be the fundamental fluid principle that can dissolve solid metals</term> dissolves the sulfur <note>original: "Schwäbel" (Schwefel)</note> which is added and present with it. This dissolution is nothing other than an ordering of the moist with the dry, and is actually the stage of **putrefaction** <term>Putrefaction: The stage of "rotting" or breaking down the substance, symbolized by the color black (nigredo), which alchemists believed was necessary for rebirth and purification</term>, and the same will make the matter <note>original: "Materiam"</note> turn black.

# The Second Article.

The second is <term>coagulation<note>The process of solidifying or thickening a liquid into a solid state; in alchemy, this is the "fixing" of the volatile spirit.</note></term>, which hardens the water again into a **body**, and it is as much as to say: that the <term>sulfur<note>original: "schwebel". It is necessary that other and many kinds of colors show themselves; for when the property of the active agent changes, it must be transformed by the capacity of the living thing. For this reason, in the <term>dissolution<note>The stage of breaking down a substance into its elemental liquid form.</note></term>, the living silver is like the active agent, but in the coagulation it is the passive subject in which the work is performed. # The Second Article.

## The Third Article.

## The Fourth Article

The last, or fourth point, that is required is that this water be separated from the earth, and then again be reunited or joined together with the earth, so that one follows the other. This must occur if the Stone <note>The "Philosopher’s Stone," the legendary substance alchemists sought to create to achieve transmutation and longevity.</note> is to be perfected. For everything that is gathered together in natural things, or joined into one body <note>original: *Corpus*</note>, exists so that it may become a single composite <note>original: *Compositum*; a substance made of several distinct parts.</note>. Within these four mentioned points <note>original: *Articuln*</note> is contained everything about which the philosophers <note>original: *Philosophi*; here referring to the ancient and medieval natural philosophers and alchemists.</note> have filled the entire world with countless books.

Splendor of the Sun.

### Of the Government of Fire.

Next follows the government of the fire: once a thing is prepared by heat, if its order is not disturbed, its nature transforms into the Sun. This is as much as to say that the spiritual is made bodily, or beautiful, and they may be gathered together. Of these two planets <note>the Sun and the Moon</note>, Senior <note>Zadith ben Hamuel, a 10th-century alchemical author</note> speaks thus: "I am a hot and dry Sun, and you, Luna <note>the Moon</note>, are cold and moist; and when we shall ascend into the noblest state, a burning light will be poured into us." This means that through the teaching and mastery of the ancients, the renewal of moisture is received, and Sun and Moon become translucent. In the <term>Ladder of the Philosophers <note>original: "scala phisicorum"; a reference to the stages or degrees of the alchemical process</note></term> it is written thus of the fire: the heat or the fire of the entire work is of a single form. For some say that the heat of the first regime should be like the heat of a brooding hen; others say it should be like the natural heat used in the digestion of food and the nourishment of the body; some say like the heat of the Sun when it is in Aries <note>the Ram; the beginning of Spring</note>. Although the Stone is completed without such specific effects, the required skill nevertheless changes. It should be a gentle and moderate heat that warms until the matter turns black and then shifts into whiteness. This is compared to the heat of the Sun when it is in Aries and begins to enter Taurus <note>the Bull</note>. When the whiteness appears, the heat shall be increased until the complete drying or calcination <note>original: "Eschierung," the process of reducing a substance to ash</note> of the Stone; and this heat becomes equal to the heat of the Sun when it is in Taurus and also in Gemini <note>the Twins</note>. And when the Stone is now dried and calcined, the fire is strengthened once more until the Stone is perfectly Red and released from the fire clothed in royal garments; and this heat is compared to the heat of the Sun when it is in Leo <note>the Lion</note>, which is the highest dignity of its house <note>the height of Summer when the Sun is strongest</note>.

# On the Colors that Appear in the Preparation of the Stone.

Miraldua the philosopher says in the *Turba* <note>the *Turba Philosophorum* or "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts</note>, it turns black twice, it yields itself twice, and it becomes red twice, and it takes on many kinds of colors. According to these colors, the heat is changed. And although many colors appear, there are only three principal ones, and these are the main colors: namely Black, White, and Red. Between these, various colors appear. Concerning the stage after the white and the first redness, Meiraldus reports—not because it is a significant stage, for it is not a perfect color, as Ciliator <note>Pietro d'Abano, a 13th-century physician and alchemist known as "the Conciliator"</note> says—that they remain in the <term>Matter <note>the physical substance being transformed in the alchemical vessel</note></term> barely long enough to be seen. But the other yellowish color, which results after the perfect white and before the final redness, shows itself for some time in the Matter; therefore, some philosophers have also considered it a main color. Miraldua speaks as noted above: these intermediate colors do not show themselves as long as the Blackness, Whiteness, and Redness, which remain in the Matter for over four days. The Blackness and Redness come twice. In every case, the perfect color is Black, which arises in the gentlest heat. Regarding this, Senior <note>Zadith ben Hamuel, a 10th-century alchemist</note> and Ciliator speak thus: "When the cooking has occurred in the gentle warmth until the Blackness fades from it." And therefore Lucas the philosopher says in the *Turba*: "Beware of strong fire, for if you make an excessive fire in the beginning, it will turn Red before its time, and that is of no use to you." For that reason, in the beginning of its rule you should have the Blackness, then the Whiteness, and finally the Redness.

Baldus the philosopher says in the *Turba* thus: "Cook your composition until you see it white, and quench it in the vinegar, and separate the blackness from the whiteness." For the whiteness is a sign and approaches <term>Fixation <note>the stage where the substance becomes stable and no longer evaporates or changes when heated</note></term>. It also requires that it be drawn away from the blackness through the fire of <term>Calcination <note>the process of heating a substance to a high temperature to effect a chemical change or reduce it to a fine powder</note></term>. For by increasing the heat, the superfluous parts are thus separated, and there remains a coarse earth or "father" of the matter, which is like a

# Of the properties of the entire work of preparing the Stone.

## SIXTH TREATISE.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'D' featuring scrolling foliage and floral patterns.</image-desc>
**Calcination** is placed at the beginning of the work, acting as the Father in a lineage, and it is three-fold: two parts belong to the **Body**, and the third to the **Spirit**. The first is a preparation of the cold moisture, which protects the wood <note>In alchemical allegory, "wood" often represents the combustible or base elements of the matter being treated</note> so that it does not burn, and this is the beginning of our work. The second is a fatty moisture that causes the wood to burn. And the third is an ashing, or <term>Incineration<note>The process of reducing a substance to ashes through prolonged heating</note></term> of the dry Earth, which gives a true Fixation <note>The process by which a volatile substance is rendered stable and resistant to fire</note> and a subtle moisture; of this there is also very little, and it produces no flame, but results in a Clear Body, like glass. In such a manner the Philosophers command their Calcination to be performed, and this is accomplished with the <term>Permanent Water<note>original: "Aqua permanente"; a specialized alchemical solvent, often referring to mercury or a treated acidic water</note></term> or <term>Sharpest Vinegar<note>original: "Acceto acerrimia"; likely a reference to a potent distilled acid used for dissolving metals</note></term>. A similar moisture exists within the metals, for it is the origin of all soft things; therefore, the <term>Calcination<note>original: "Calcinierung"; the reduction of a solid to powder by heat</note></term> of the Philosophers is an indication of the destruction of the [raw] moisture and the introduction of another fatty moisture, from which the essentiality or <term>Quintessence<note>original: "Quinta Essentia"; the "fifth essence," the purest and most concentrated form of a substance</note></term> and life arise. For this reason it is called a softening <note>original: "schmeisung," likely implying a melting or making-malleable</note>, which occurs with the water of the Philosophers; this is actually the <term>Sublimation<note>The process where a substance is heated into vapor and then condensed back into a solid</note></term>, or the Philosophers' <term>Resolution<note>original: "Resolution"; the breaking down or dissolving of a substance into its component parts</note></term>, for through it the hard dryness is altered, and a softening occurs in which the dryness is drawn out—the <term>Quintessence</term>, or the separation of the elements. And this happens so that the parts which were killed by the fire, and
