...pressed together, they have become subtle through the Spirit, which is a <term>dissolving water<note>original: "Resolvierends Wasser"; a solvent capable of breaking down solid matter into its spiritual or liquid essence</note></term> and a moisture of the destroyed bodies. With the introduction of the destroyed heat, an airy dissolution occurs, and that is the implantation of the elements.

Therefore, **Sublimation** means that the coarse earthiness is made vaporous or subtle, and is turned into the moisture of the Water, and the warmth of the Air, and the moisture of the Air, and the heat of the Fire. This is a conversion of the elements, where the extracted <term>Fifth Essence<note>original: "Quinta Essentia"; the purest, most concentrated essence of a substance, beyond the four classical elements</note></term> is separated from the elements and from the <term>dregs<note>original: "Fecibus"; the useless sediment or waste matter remaining after distillation or filtration</note></term>. This Fifth Essence is an effective moisture of a very high nature that tinctures <note>To "tincture" in alchemy is to permanently change the color and nature of a base metal into gold or silver</note> indestructibly. It is also the true **Fixation** of which <note>Geber, or Jabir ibn Hayyan, was a legendary 8th-century polymath often called the "Father of Chemistry"</note> **Geber** speaks: nothing becomes fixed unless it be illuminated and becomes a beautiful, transparent substance. For it is there that the **Philosophers' Sulfur** <note>original: "Sulphur philosophorum"</note>—or the extracted Ash—arises; without this, the entire mastery is in vain. It is a metallic water that rejoices in the body and makes it alive; it is an **Elixir** of the White and Red Tincture, and a Tincturing Spirit. In this <term>washing<note>original: "Ablutio"; the purification of the matter, often associated with the transition from the black stage to the white stage</note></term>, the blackness and the stench are removed; the matter is made dead and then alive again when a pure, indestructible heat and metallic moisture are introduced, from which it gains its tincturing power.

Then the philosophical **Putrefaction** or rotting is accomplished, which was mentioned at the beginning of this booklet. By this process, that which was previously manifest is destroyed, and the hidden is brought forth, of which the <note>The *Turba Philosophorum* (Assembly of the Philosophers) is one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts</note> ***Turba*** speaks. Rotting is the first step and reveals the greatest secrets; it is also the true separation of the elements—that is, to transform them. Regarding this, the *Turba* says: "Convert the elements; what is moist, make dry, and what is moist, make fixed." And it further says: "When everything is crushed to powder, it is prepared with diligence," and that is the "grinding of the philosophers." Therefore, <note>Senior Zadith (Ibn Umail) was a 10th-century Arabic alchemist whose works were highly regarded in medieval Europe</note> **Senior** says: "**Calcination** is of no use unless a powder comes from it."

# Splendor Solis.

There is also the **Cooking** <note>original: "Kochung"; in alchemy, this refers to "digestion," the process of exposing a substance to gentle, continuous heat to mature it</note> of which all philosophers speak, especially **Albertus Magnus** <note>A 13th-century German bishop and philosopher who was legendary for his supposed mastery of alchemy</note>, who says: among all arts, there is none that follows Nature so closely as **Alchemy**, and that is because of the cooking and the **Forming** <note>original: "Formierung"; the process by which the "form" or essence of a substance is established in the matter</note>. For it is cooked in the fiery and red metallic water, which mostly comes from the Sun and a little from the Matter. There is also the **Philosophers’ Roasting** <note>original: "Assation" or "Brattung"; a method of drying a substance over a fire without adding liquid, often compared to parching</note>, for that same moisture is consumed with a gentle fire. Above all, one must take care that the spirit—which dries out from the body and is dried by the body—is not lost or opposed to the body, or it will not be perfect.

There is also the **Philosophers’ Distillation** or **Clarification**, which is nothing other than the purification of a <margin>x</margin> thing with its subtle moisture. And with **Coagulation** <note>The process of thickening or solidifying a liquid into a solid state</note>, the philosophers concluded the entire work. Of this **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical father of alchemy; this quote refers to the Emerald Tablet</note> speaks: "Its nursing mother is the Sun." This means: its power is complete when it is changed into a constant earth. There are also countless other effects, as follows hereafter, that may result from it; yet it is nothing other than that everything natural is fulfilled by the Air. For the art which follows Nature in truth—and not in mere imitation as other arts do—is confirmed by **Senior** <note>Senior Zadith, the Latinized name of the 10th-century alchemist Zadith ben Hamuel</note> when he says: "He does not live, who can complete this art without Nature." Yes, I say: with such a Nature which is poured into Nature from heaven above.

# On the manifold effects of the entire work, also how the philosophers have so many names and comparisons in this art of the preparation of the Blessed Stone

## SEVENTH TREATISE.

<image-desc>A large decorative drop cap 'E' featuring intricate floral and foliage patterns within a square border.</image-desc>

It is a common proverb among all philosophers: he who knows how to kill <note>original: "tödten"; in alchemy, to "kill" a substance means to "fix" it, or change it from a volatile, liquid state (like mercury) into a solid, stable state that can withstand fire.</note> the Quicksilver <note>original: "Lebendige Silber," literally "Living Silver."</note> is a master in this art. However, great diligence must be applied to their Mercury, for they describe it in many ways. **Senior** <note>Senior Zadith, the Latinized name of the 10th-century Arab alchemist Ibn Umail, whose "Tabula Chemica" was a major influence.</note> speaks thus: "Our fire is a water; if you can give a fire to a fire, and a Mercury to a Mercury, then you have done enough." For he calls the Quicksilver both a water and a fire, and the fire must be made with fire. Likewise, he says: the soul is drawn out through putrefaction <note>original: "feülung"; the process of decomposition or "blackening" (nigredo) that was thought to release the spirit from the matter.</note>, and when nothing more of the soul remains [in the matter], then you have already washed the body; that is a soul and a body.

Likewise, it is called the <term>Fifth Essence</term> <note>original: "Quinta Essentia"; the celestial essence or "ether" that exists beyond the four earthly elements.</note>, or a spirit, <term>Permanent Water</term> <note>original: "Aqua permanens"; a metaphorical name for the secret solvent that dissolves metals without wetting the hands.</note>, or <term>Menstruum</term> <note>original: "Menstrum"; a solvent used for extraction, often associated with cyclical time and the blood of the "Philosophical Lion."</note>. She speaks thus: take the Quicksilver and the body of <term>Magnesia</term> <note>A term for the "Primal Matter" or the mineral body from which the stone is extracted, not to be confused with modern magnesium.</note>, or a sulfur that does not burn, and dissolve <note>original: "zertreib"; literally to disperse or grind down.</note> it in the sharpest vinegar. In that vinegar, it will become neither black, nor white, nor red-colored; and thus it becomes a "killed" quicksilver, and is of a water-color before the fire is added to it; for then it becomes red within it. Thus speaks the <term>Assembly</term> <note>original: "Turba," referring to the *Turba Philosophorum* (The Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the earliest Latin alchemical texts.</note>, laying it into the gold; then it becomes an <term>Elixir</term> <note>A prepared substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold or curing diseases.</note>, and is of its <term>Tincture</term> <note>The transmuting power or "dyeing" quality of the Stone that changes the nature of other metals.</note>

From white <term>Lead</term> make a white <term>Tincture</term>, and thus you have begun the work of wisdom. Although the <term>Philosopher</term> <note>Often referring to Aristotle, though here likely a general reference to alchemical authority.</note> says that nothing is closer to <term>Gold</term> than <term>Lead</term>, for within it is life, and it draws all secrets to itself; however, this is not spoken of common <term>Lead</term>. Likewise, the <term>Marcasite</term> <note>original: "Marcosit"; a metallic mineral often confused with pyrite.</note>—because the "stinking earth" gains glowing sparks from it, as <term>Morienes</term> <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist who reportedly taught the secrets of the stone to King Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says—is also compared to <term>Arsenic</term>, <term>Orpiment</term> <note>original: "Auripigmento"; a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral.</note>, and <term>Tutty</term> <note>original: "Tutia"; zinc oxide gathered from the flues of smelting furnaces.</note>. Likewise, it is compared to many things that are not <term>Mineral</term> at all, but come from the four <term>Complexions</term> <note>The four humors or temperaments: sanguine, choleric, melancholic, and phlegmatic.</note>, the <term>Basilisk</term> <note>original: "Basiliseo"; a mythical king of serpents, here representing a potent alchemical substance or "poison."</note>, blood, and many such superfluous things; and among <term>Mineral</term> things, to <term>Salt</term>, <term>Alum</term>, and others, because of their many different properties.

But before all things, <term>Alphidius</term> <note>An Arabic alchemist whose aphorisms were highly regarded in the Middle Ages.</note> warns us and says: "Dear son, guard yourself against the <term>Spiritual Bodies</term> and stones that are dead, as mentioned above; for in them is no path, nor will you find your purpose or design, for their power does not increase but becomes nothing." But the <term>Philosophers' Salt</term>, which is a <term>Tincture</term>, is extracted like other <term>Alkali Salts</term> <note>original: "Salalkuli"</note> from the <term>Body</term>. This also happens when it is extracted from the <term>Body</term> of <term>Metals</term>, about which <term>Senior</term> <note>Senior Zadith (Ibn Umail), a 10th-century philosopher whose work "The Silvery Water and the Earthly Star" was foundational to later alchemy.</note> says: First it becomes like an ash, thereafter a <term>Salt</term>, and through manifold labor it becomes at last a <term>Mercury of the Philosophers</term> <note>original: "Mercurio Philosophorum"; the perfected, living essence of the metal.</note>; but primarily <term>Sal-ammoniac</term> <note>original: "Salarmoniac"; ammonium chloride, prized for its ability to sublimate and dissolve metals.</note> is the best and noblest of all that exists.

<term>Arles</term> <note>Likely a reference to the alchemical author Arisleus.</note> in the *Book of the Seven Commandments* speaks thus: "<term>Almisadier</term> <note>An Arabic term for sal-ammoniac.</note>, that is <term>Sal-ammoniac</term>, shall serve you alone; for it dissolves <term>Bodies</term> and makes them soft and spiritual." The <term>Turba</term> <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, an ancient alchemical assembly text.</note> also intends this with these words: "You should know that it does not tint the <term>Bodies</term> unless the <term>Spirit</term> which lies hidden in its belly is drawn out." Then it becomes a water and a <term>Body</term> which is of a spiritual nature. Therefore, it does not tint the thick, earthly thing, but that which is prepared is of a thin nature and color; but the <term>Spirit</term>, which is of a watery nature, tints into an <term>Elixir</term>.

And because of this, that which is drawn out of it is a White and Red, truthful <term>Fixation</term> <note>original: "Fixation"; the process of making a volatile substance stable so it can withstand the heat of fire without evaporating.</note> of perfect colors, a penetrating <term>Tincture</term> <note>original: "Tinctur"; the elixir or "medicine" of the stone that transforms base metals into gold.</note> that mixes itself among all metals.

The perfection of the entire <term>Masterpiece</term> <note>original: "Meisterschafft"; referring to the completion of the "Great Work" (Magnum Opus).</note> depends on this single point: that one should extract the <term>Sulfur</term> <note>original: "Schwäffel"; in alchemy, sulfur represents the active, masculine, and combustible principle, rather than just the yellow chemical element.</note> from the perfect bodies, which possess the <term>Fixed Death</term> <note>original: "Fixen Mortem"; a state of stability where the matter has been "killed" or calcined and is no longer subject to change or volatility.</note>. For this Sulfur is their oldest and most subtle part in the form of <term>Crystalline Salt</term>, sweet and flavorful, and a radical moisture <note>original: "wurßenliche feuchtigkeit"; the fundamental life-fluid believed to exist within all matter.</note>. If these remain in the fire for a year, they will always be like a melted wax; and therefore a small part hardens a large mass of common <term>Mercury</term> <note>original: "Quecksilber"</note> into a truthful <term>Gold</term>. Therefore, the moisture or water that is extracted <margin>X</margin> <note>The marginal 'X' likely indicates a key procedural step in the manuscript.</note> from the metallic bodies is called the <term>Soul</term>—the Soul of the Stone. <term>Mercury</term>, however, or its power, is called the <term>Spirit</term> when it takes on a sulfurous nature. And the digested Earth is the <term>Body</term> and the corpus of the <term>Fifth Essence</term> <note>original: "Quinta Essentia"; the purest and most concentrated essence of a substance, transcending the four physical elements.</note> and the final Tincture. These three are a single thing from a single root, differing only in their effects. The names of these things are countably many, yet everything concerns one single thing; they are like a chain, joined and linked to one another, so that when one ends, another begins.

Firstly, it preserves humans from all kinds of diseases.

Thirdly, it transforms all gemstones.

Regarding the **First** [virtue], the wise **Philosophers** say: if one takes this same [medicine] in a warm drink—wine or water—it restores health in that very hour. Specifically, it cures **paralysis** <note>original: "Paraliticum"</note>, **dropsy** <note>original: "Wassersucht"; an accumulation of fluid in the body</note>, leprosy, jaundice, heart palpitations, **intestinal colic** <note>original: "Darmgicht"</note>, fever, **epilepsy** <note>original: "Fallendesucht"; literally 'the falling sickness'</note>, **stomach cramps** <note>original: "Grimmen"</note>, and many other internal ailments of the body. It also heals the outside of the body if one anoints themselves with it. It removes harmful fluids from an unhealthy stomach, as well as all **melancholy** and gloominess. It also wards off all diseases of the eyes, strengthens the heart, restores hearing, makes teeth sound, brings life back to paralyzed limbs, and heals all **abscesses** <note>original: "Apostemata"</note> as well as all external injuries: fistulas, cancer, **lupus** <note>original: "Wolff"; historically referring to skin ulcers or 'the wolf' that eats the flesh</note>. In summary, it may be taken internally, or used as a powder or ointment. **Senior** <note>referring to Senior Zadith, a famous 10th-century Arabian alchemist often cited in European texts</note> says: it makes a person joyful and young, and keeps the body fresh and healthy against internal and external infirmities. Therefore, it is a medicine above all other medicines of **Hippocrates**, **Galen**, **Constantine**, **Alexander**, **Avicenna**, and many other scholars, all of whom it surpasses.

One should also mix this medicine with other medicines or waters that are suited to and combat the specific illness.

Of the **Second** virtue, it is written that it transforms all imperfect metals. This is evident, for it makes any silver entirely into gold—in its color, its substance, and in its weight—permanently.

Of the **Third**, it is written that this medicine also creates other stones such as **Jasper**, **Hyacinth**, White and Red **Coral**, **Emerald**, **Chrysolite**, and **Sapphire**. Likewise, from crystals, it creates **Carbuncle**, **Ruby**, and **Topaz** <note>original: "Theopasius"</note>, which are much better and more powerful than the natural ones; and this medicine also melts all precious stones.

## Concluding Discourse

This most precious art and comforter of the poor, the noble **Alchemy** <term>Alchymia; the medieval forerunner of chemistry, focused on the transformation of matter and the soul</term>, is above all natural arts that humans may ever possess on Earth. It is to be regarded as a gift from God, for it is mostly hidden by the ancient sages in manifold sayings, figurative riddles, and parables <note>original: "Gleichnuſſen"; the alchemical tradition heavily used allegories like "the Green Lion" or "the King" to hide secrets from the uninitiated</note>. For the philosopher **Senior** <note>Senior Zadith, the Latinized name of the 10th-century Arabic alchemist Muhammad ibn Umail al-Tamimi</note> says: A person of understanding will soon perceive or understand this art if they contemplate it, provided their mind and spirit are illuminated by the books of knowledge of this art.

Therefore, whoever wishes to act wisely should seek the wisdom of the ancient sages, which practices and proceeds through the agility of various parables, distinctions, and secrets. Through these, they describe their operations and descriptions in hidden words and riddles, grounded and established in contemplation. For reflection is a subtle sense, and to those alone who have understanding in these things, it is entirely easy and natural.

However, regarding those who have no understanding of these matters—as Senior also says—nothing is more contemptible. But he who possesses the art is as rich as one who has a flint to make fire; from it, he strikes fire and gives fire when, how much, and to whom he wishes, without any loss to the fire or the flint. In this way, it is also possible to give in abundance. Rich gold—it is better for a person than all the world's goods, merchandise, gold, and silver. Its fruits are better than all the wealth of the world, because through it is accomplished that which requires long life and health; for its final fruits are the true **Drinkable Gold** <note>original: "Aurum potabile"; a legendary alchemical medicine consisting of gold dissolved in a liquid, believed to grant immortality or perfect health</note>.

The most precious Art and comforter of the poor, the noble Alchemy, which stands above all natural arts that men may ever have on Earth, is to be regarded as a gift from God; for it is mostly hidden in the manifold sayings, figurative circumlocutions, and parables of the ancient sages. Mirror of Alchemy.

## Preface.

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'V' featuring intricate floral and scrollwork patterns.</image-desc>Many and various were the ways that the <term>Philosophers<note>In alchemical texts, "Philosophers" refers to the practitioners of alchemy, often called "Natural Philosophers."</note></term> spoke with one another in times past through their writings, just as if in darkness; and with a foggy voice they have left us obscured regarding an <term>Art<note>The "Art" or "Noblest Art" is a standard term for Alchemy itself.</note></term> above all other arts, the noblest, and as if under a shadow of doubt. They did not do this without cause, for they did not wish their writings to become a benefit or a common utility to any but their own children <note>The "children of the art" or "sons of Hermes" were the initiated students of alchemy.</note> and those strangers who were not ignorant of the truth, provided they had previously discussed such things by word of mouth. They also covered and hid such things from one another in the secrecy of the faith. And all that which they encountered hereafter in their <term>parables<note>original: "Paraboln"; alchemists used allegories, myths, and metaphors (parables) to hide their recipes from the uninitiated.</note></term> to one another, they understood amongst themselves through those same parables; thus, they had no need for open speech with one another, nor with their other dear friends, nor did they require a more certain assurance.

Secondly, they did not want the <term>Gift of God<note>original: "Gabe Gottes"; the secret of the Philosopher's Stone was considered a divine gift that could not be attained through labor alone, but required God's favor.</note></term> and the secret of the Art to be revealed and discovered, and they took care that the wicked should never attain it. It is for those alone who possess the Art, to whom God especially reveals it and gives it as they deserve. For the Art would be given in vain, or uselessly, to ignorant and senseless men. Therefore, for those who are worthy and desire to work in this Art, we wish to give and write the entire, perfect Art in plain truth, bare and uncovered, and without the intrusion or interference of foggy speech; we wish to lead them in by a nearby path and bring them to an infinite joy.

And for that reason, I will write this and divide it into seven chapters, neither too few nor too many, but only what is
<meta>catchword: necessary <note>original: "Not"; likely the start of "Nothdurfft" (necessity).</note></meta>

<summary>In this preface, Poyselius explains that while previous alchemists used "foggy" parables to hide their secrets from the wicked and ignorant, he intends to write a clear, seven-chapter guide for the worthy. He frames alchemy as a "Gift of God" that should only be shared with those who deserve it.</summary>
<keywords>Preface, Philosophers, Alchemical Art, Parables, Gift of God, Secrecy, Seven Chapters, Ulrich Poyselius</keywords>

->H 3<-
<meta>catchword: than</note>

It is both necessary and useful to know that I will write for you seven clear chapters, in which you will finally find the mastery of our meaning and intent. Within these, your understanding will be continually increased in subtlety. A clear and subtle enlightenment is always found among the <term>Philosophers<note>The "Philosophers" are the historical alchemists and natural scientists who sought the secrets of nature.</note></term>, whereas among the peasants, one finds only a peasant-like coarseness and lack of refinement. In these seven chapters—if you will look upon them diligently and review them with constant, industrious study—you will find the sense and meaning of Philosophy and the entire understanding of the Art upon which you may establish and ground yourself. You may proceed upon this foundation quite powerfully and steadily, until through constant practice, you have drawn out the meaning and the work according to your full will.

I have promised the Art without any omission and also without any excess, which I will write here perfectly and openly without any doubt. This is for those who have previously worked a little in <term>sublimation<note>The process of heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then back into a solid, used to purify substances.</note></term>, <term>descension<note>A method of distillation where the vapors are forced downward into a receiving vessel.</note></term>, <term>distillation<note>The purification of a liquid by heating it into vapor and then condensing it back into a liquid.</note></term>, <term>fixation<note>The process of making a volatile substance "fixed" or stable so that it no longer evaporates when heated.</note></term>, <term>calcination<note>Heating a substance to a high temperature in the air to reduce it to a powder or ash.</note></term>, <term>solution<note>Dissolving a solid substance into a liquid state.</note></term>, <term>coagulation<note>The thickening or solidifying of a liquid or a dissolved substance.</note></term>, and <term>incorporation<note>The thorough mixing or combining of different substances into a single body.</note></term>, and in other manipulations and endless deceptions. Although these terms are named and written everywhere in all the books of the Philosophers and also in other deceptive books, I say finally to those who work in the retreating and deceptive arts—such as in the four <term>spirits<note>original: "Spiritibus"; in alchemy, these are volatile substances like mercury, sulfur, arsenic, and sal ammoniac.</note></term> of <term>Alchemy</term>, and in the seven <term>metals<note>The seven classical metals: Gold, Silver, Mercury, Copper, Iron, Tin, and Lead.</note></term>, and also in <term>salts</term>, <term>alums<note>original: "Aluminibus"; various mineral salts used in alchemical processes.</note></term>, <term>borax</term>, and <term>atraments<note>original: "Atramenten"; a group of black, ink-like substances or vitriols.</note></term>, as well as in all types of <term>marcasites<note>Metallic minerals, often iron pyrites, used in experiments.</note></term>, <term>tutty<note>A crude zinc oxide collected from smelting furnaces.</note></term>, magnets or <term>magnesia<note>likely referring to various mineral ores or magnets used to "attract" the hidden spirits of metals.</note></term>, and also in many other <term>mineral</term> things, and also in many <term>vegetables<note>original: "Vegetabilibus"; refers to organic or plant-based substances.</note></term> (that is, in growing things) and in other endless things from which they cannot come to a happy end—that they have nevertheless [through this book] come to a true knowledge. That is: there is one thing, one Stone, and one Way, with which the entire mastery is completed.

Therefore, I command you that you guard yourself against all others...

# Mirror of Alchemy.

...other writings, and guide yourself toward these seven chapters, which entirely contain within them the transformation of metals. Upon these, you may powerfully establish your foundation. If you often contemplate in your heart their beginning, middle, and end, you will find therein such a subtlety that your spirit will be fulfilled.

First, it is asked: what is alchemy, and why was it invented?

Second, concerning the beginning of natural things, and from what substances metals are created and born.

# Mirror of Alchemy.

# The First Chapter.

## The description of the art and explanation of Alchemy, and what it truly is.

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial 'I' featuring scrollwork and foliate patterns.</image-desc>
In many and more old books and writings of the philosophers, there is found quite openly the description and explanation of this same art; therefore, we must also take note in this first chapter of this same opinion and explanation. Regarding this, Hermes the Philosopher <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure often credited as the founder of alchemy and the author of the "Hermetic" corpus.</note> writes to us and explains it thus: Alchemy is an art of metals, or metallic things, made out of one and through one, simply composed, and also a joining together of the most noble things which overcome one another through knowledge and activity; and through this same natural mixing, it will transform the nature of metals, changing them into something better.

Another philosopher writes thus: Alchemy is an art that teaches how to transform every kind of metal, one into the other. And this must happen through its own <term>Medicine<note>original: "Medicininam" or "Artzney". In an alchemical context, "Medicine" refers to the transformative substance used to "heal" or perfect base metals into gold.</note></term>, which is evident and written in many books of the philosophers. And regarding this, it should be known that Alchemy is such an art that is so named after a philosopher who was called Achymus <note>A legendary figure often cited in early modern texts as the namesake of "Alchemy," though modern etymology traces the word back through Arabic and Greek roots.</note>; and the art teaches how to make a medicine, which is called an <term>Elixir<note>The "Elixir" (or Philosopher's Stone) is the legendary substance sought by alchemists to transform base metals into gold and provide longevity.</note></term>. This same Elixir, when it is cast upon the imperfect metals, makes them perfect and good; that is the reason for its invention.

## The Second Chapter.

### On the Origin of Metals:

In the words just written, I have fulfilled and completed the first chapter, and now in the second, I will fully explain the origin of <term>minerals <note>original: "Minerum"</note></term> or the ore of the mines—how and from what they naturally first sprang and were created. Regarding this, it is first to be noted that the origin of minerals, ore, or mine-works is nothing other than <term>☿ <note>Mercury (quicksilver)</note></term> and Sulphur; from these two things all <term>metals <note>original: "Metalla"</note></term> are created and born.

Therefore, there are many and varied forms, and one is transformed differently than the other; but Nature has always had the intention and set it before herself to make Gold. However, the contrary and various flaws that occur result in the creation of many different and opposing metals through transformation, as is then quite clearly written and found in many books of the philosophers. For according to whether the two aforementioned Sulphur and <term>☿ <note>Mercury</note></term> are pure or impure, accordingly the metals are also created or born—such as Gold, Silver, Copper, Lead, Tin, and Iron.

Now to write of Gold: it is a perfect and pure metal, created and born out of a pure and <term>fixed <note>Stable and resistant to the heat of fire.</note></term> Sulphur that is clear and red; it has no defect in it. Silver is a pure metal and nearly perfect, yet not entirely so; it is created out of a pure and almost fixed <term>Mercury <note>original: "☿"</note></term>, and out of a clear, white, and almost fixed Sulphur. It lacks a little <term>cooking <note>original: "Kochung"; the alchemical process of maturation or "digestion" within the earth.</note></term> and fixation, and it also lacks in color and in weight. Tin is an impure metal, and it is created out of a pure Mercury and a Sulphur that is partly fixed and clear, and also out of a Sulphur that is in part pure and clear

# The Third Chapter.

## Here follows further upon what the Elixir shall be made of.

In the aforementioned and now proven writings, it has been sufficiently described and completed regarding the creation of metals, both the perfect and the imperfect. Therefore, we wish to return to the making and accomplishing of the **Medicines of metals**. We have now been sufficiently and clearly informed in the preceding chapters that all **metals** are created and grown from **Mercury** and **Sulphur**. It is the purity or impurity of these two that accomplishes or <unclear>zerzit</unclear> the metals and makes them perfect or imperfect. There is also nothing in the world that can attach to metals, or may affect them, or cause a darkness within them, unless it be composed of these two or has sprung from them. It is now established that no external thing is able or sufficient to improve metals, to make them perfect, or to create any kind of transformation in them from new substances. Therefore, it is to be wondered at that a <term>subtle man <note>Meaning a learned or clever scholar.</note></term>, who thinks himself certain of his knowledge, would base his foundation and opinion upon **Vegetables** <note>original: "Vegetabilia"; refers to the plant kingdom or organic matter.</note>, which are growing things, or upon other foreign things; for there are enough **minerals** found in **ore** or **mines** that are close to the metallic nature.

You should by no means believe or consider that the **Philosophers** <note>Refers to the ancient and medieval alchemical authorities.</note> have established or written of the Art in the aforementioned foreign things, except only as a <term>parable <note>original: "Gleichnuß"; an allegory or metaphor used to hide secrets from the uninitiated.</note></term>. For from the two substances mentioned before—that is, <term>Mercury <note>original: "☿"</note></term> and **Sulphur**—all metals have sprung and are born. Nothing else attaches to them, and nothing else is added to them; nor can anything else effect a transformation in them...

The author warns against taking the allegorical language of older alchemical texts too literally.</summary>

...[they] have nothing superfluous or too much; and if their perfection were mixable with the imperfect metals, would the imperfect **metals** <note>original: "Metalla"</note> not also be diminished and corrupted by the perfect ones when they are mixed together in the flow <note>Referring to the molten state of metals during smelting or melting.</note>?

Only if it should happen that they are dissolved into their **primary matter** <note>original: "erste Materiam"; the base elemental state of a substance before it takes a specific form.</note>, which is to say that they should become **volatile** <note>original: "flüchtig"; meaning easily evaporated or transformed into vapor by heat.</note> with the volatile, when the greater part of the volatile exceeds [the rest], and it rises with that which is more **Fixed** <note>original: "Fix"; referring to a substance that is stable in fire and does not evaporate.</note>.

And likewise for **Luna** <note>The alchemical name for Silver, associated with the Moon.</note>, that is silver, why do we not take it for the white **Elixir**? The reason we take neither of these two is because these two **Bodies** or metals are so powerfully and perfectly **fixed** <note>original: "gefigiert"; rendered solid and resistant to fire.</note>, and are so strongly cooked and divided with equal natural fires, that it will not easily or at all come to pass that we, with our knowledge and mastery, can or may work or labor upon anything within them.

And if we now wished to make our **Elixir** out of the two perfect metals, we would have to bring them back into their **primary nature**, which would be very difficult for us to accomplish. And although nature accomplishes something and makes it perfect, it cannot bring that same thing any higher or purge <note>To purify or refine.</note> it within its innermost nature beyond what it itself requires and what is necessary for it.

## The Fourth Chapter.

### Why the Art is to be practiced.

Even if you are darkened by such a coarse and hard understanding and by ignorance, you shall find in the transcribed chapters our true and manifest meaning: which is the right and true **Matter** <note>original: "Materi"</note> of our **Elixir** <term>Elixir</term> <note>A substance or "medicine" capable of curing the "diseases" of metals—that is, their impurities—to turn them into gold.</note>. Thus we must take up and note the operation and its nature, and we must also direct ourselves accordingly.

We see clearly in minerals or ores—that is, in the mines—that through a steady heat which is enclosed within the mountains, the water becomes coarse and thick. ## The Fifth Chapter.

In plain and uncovered words, I have certainly [described] the matter <note>original: "Materiam"</note>, and also the meaning and the way to work. Now, to speak of the vessel and the furnace—how and from what they should be made—it is now to be noted that as Nature cooks the metals in the mountains with her natural fire, that same cooking cannot and may not happen without a vessel or an instrument suitable for it. And if we intend and have the will to follow Nature in this cooking, why should we then not also use a vessel or container for it? Let us, therefore, first look and observe what the place is where the metals are born.

Now we may quite clearly understand and perceive that in those same places, in the mountains, at the very bottom of the mountain's floor, there is a steady warmth that is always equally warm. It is the nature of warmth and its property that it always rises, desiring to go upward; and in that same rising, it makes dry and hardens all the water that it finds...

# The Seventh Chapter.

### On Projection or Tinging.

Now, concerning the promise of the perfect and masterly work—bringing the labor of the great and exceeding Elixir, both White and Red, to a perfect and useful conclusion—one must now know how the <term>projection</term> <note>original: "proiection"; the final stage of alchemy where a small amount of the "Stone" or "Elixir" is cast upon molten base metal to transform it.</note> (that is, the "throwing-on" or "tinging") should occur. This is the final task in this work, which we have awaited and expected with eager joy for a long time; regarding this, we shall provide teaching and instruction.

To speak now of the White Elixir: this White Elixir <term>tinges</term> <note>original: "tingiert"; from the Latin *tingere*, meaning to dye or permeate. In alchemy, it refers to the Elixir's power to fundamentally change the color and nature of a base metal.</note> without limit, and it transforms every "imperfect" metal into a perfect metal—that is, into a good, stable, and true silver. However, you must know that some metals are "further" from perfection, while others possess more of it already. Even though the Elixir tinges and perfects every metal, it transforms those metals much more easily and effectively that are already closer to perfection than those which are further away. And since we find one metal to be closer to perfection than another, we shall excuse ourselves and state clearly that we do not need to choose those metals which are far from perfection, but rather those that are near.

If you now diligently read through my chapters and consider them well, you will find revealed there quite openly—and without concealment—which metal is closer to or further from perfection than another. Without any doubt, anyone possessed of a subtle understanding who correctly notes and understands my aforementioned words will easily find upon which metal this Elixir should be thrown, and from which <term>matter</term> <note>The "Materi" or Prime Matter is the original substance the alchemist begins with.</note> the Elixir itself is to be made. ## A Closing Speech and the End of this Art.

# The Royal Water of the Philosophers.

Take vitriol <note>A term for various metal sulfates, likely iron or copper sulfate here.</note> that has been calcined <note>Heated to a high temperature to drive off volatile components, leaving a dry powder.</note> to a golden color, and saltpeter, equal parts of 2 pounds each; calcined alum 1 pound. From these, distill an *Aqua fortis* <note>original: "Aquafort"; literally "Strong Water," which is nitric acid.</note> as is the custom, and drive the spirits <note>Vapors or essences released during heating.</note> out well. Weigh this *Aqua fortis*, and for every 6 *loth* <note>A historical unit of weight, roughly equivalent to 15 grams or half an ounce.</note> of *Aqua fortis*, add 1 *loth* of sal ammoniac <note>original: "Salmiax"; ammonium chloride, used to turn nitric acid into *Aqua regia*.</note>. Let it dissolve therein, and thus you have the Royal Water of the Philosophers.

# Essentialized Mercury.

Take vitriol and saltpeter in equal parts; mix them together. Let them melt gently in an earthenware vessel until the moisture has evaporated. Grind the mass into a fine powder and place it in the bottom of a bowl or vessel. Take 1 pound of quicksilver <note>original: "Mercurium viuum"; literally "living mercury," or liquid elemental mercury.</note>, place it in a leather cloth, and squeeze a portion of it onto the powder; then place another layer of the powder on top, and proceed thus layer upon layer <note>original: "stratum super stratum."</note> until all is combined. Put this mixture into a coated flask <note>original: "beschlagnen Kolben"; a glass flask reinforced with a layer of clay or lute to withstand heat.</note> of uniform width, with a helm <note>The top part of a still.</note> luted <note>Sealed with a paste or "lute" to make it airtight.</note> on top, and sublimate <note>The process of heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again in the cooler top of the vessel.</note> the mercury out as is otherwise the custom. Then discard the dregs <note>original: "feces"; the solid residue left behind.</note> and sublimate the mercury by itself without any further additions two more times, or as often as necessary until it rises alone and leaves no more dregs behind it.

Then take the Royal Water of the Philosophers and place 1 pound of this <term>sublimated mercury <note>indicated by the symbol ☿</note></term> into a glass flask. Let it dissolve and distill it off; and once the *Aqua fortis* has been removed, drive the mercury upward <note>sublimate it again</note>. It will then resolve into a beautiful white, like snow. Discard the dregs that remain at the bottom <note>original: "infundo" (in fundo).</note> and are black, and pour the Royal Water again over the dregs,

## The Frozen Ice-Water.

Take 1 pound each of the essentialized Mercury and raw antimony <note>original: "Antimonij crudi"; a naturally occurring mineral (stibnite) used frequently in alchemy.</note>. Crush the antimony very fine, then rub the essentialized Mercury thoroughly into it. Place this immediately into a coated glass flask <note>A flask reinforced with a layer of clay or lute to withstand high heat.</note> that is neither too tall nor too wide. Upon it, place a still-head <note>original: "Helm"; the top part of a distillation apparatus.</note> with very short tubes, and a separating flask as a receiver. Let everything be well-sealed with lute <note>original: "luttiert"; a paste used to make airtight joints in chemical apparatus.</note> so that nothing can escape. Then, in a sand bath <note>original: "Sand Capellen"; a container of sand heated to provide even, controlled temperature to the glass.</note>, distill it gently at first, as one would for *Aqua fortis* <note>Nitric acid.</note>. Increase the heat for 12 hours until it becomes like *Aqua fortis*; for a <term>mercurial spirit</term> <note>original: "☿"; the symbol for Mercury.</note> will be heard coming from the antimony with a bubbling sound. First, a watery liquid <note>original: "Phlegma"; an alchemical term for a watery, low-potency distillate.</note> will come over like an oil, and then the frozen ice-water will pass over like icicles <note>A description of a substance solidifying in the neck of the still, likely antimony trichloride, known as "Butter of Antimony."</note>. Keep this oil and the icicles carefully together; this is the frozen ice-water from which springs the Mercurial Water of the Philosophers <note>original: "Aqua Mercurialis Philosophorum."</note> and the common Mercury of Life <note>original: "Mercurius vitæ"; a white powder (antimony oxychloride) used medicinally.</note>, of which you may make as much as you desire.

## Mercurial Water of the Philosophers.

Take as much of the frozen ice-water as you wish, along with its oiliness, and distill it by itself <note>original: "per se."</note> without any further additions. Do this twice more in a vial, and then you have the Mercurial Water of the Philosophers.

# Mercury of Common Life <note>original: "Mercurius vitæ communis"; in the Paracelsian tradition, this is not actual mercury, but a highly purified, "essential" substance derived through chemical manipulation, often associated with antimony.</note>

Take the frozen ice-water <note>This refers to the distillate produced on the previous page, likely antimony trichloride, which is solid at room temperature but melts easily, resembling ice.</note> together with its residue <note>original: "Glitet"; likely referring to the crystalline crust or dregs formed during the previous distillation.</note>, as much as you wish. Place it upon a clean marble slab and let it dissolve <note>original: "soluieren"; in this context, to melt or liquefy at room temperature.</note>. Afterward, place it into a low, uniformly wide, coated separating flask <note>original: "beschlagnen scheidt Kolben"; a glass vessel reinforced with a layer of clay or lute to protect it from direct heat.</note>—sized according to the quantity of the work—with its still-head <note>original: "Helm"</note> and receiver vessel, all well-sealed with lute <note>original: "verlutiert"; an airtight seal made of clay, lime, or other binding materials.</note>. Place it in a sand bath, ensuring no spirits <note>The volatile vapors produced during heating.</note> escape, until the residue appears and until a small white ring shows itself on the side of the glass and it coagulates <note>Solidifies into a mass.</note>. Then let it cool so that it sets and hardens. After this, break the glass flask and put the coagulated mass <note>original: "coagulatum"</note> back onto your marble slab to dissolve again.

Now, one must take care: if the process is overlooked and the heat is too high during this first coagulation, such that some of the subtle spirits have risen, you must take the phlegm <note>original: "Phlegma"; the watery, less-active liquid that distills over first.</note> that has passed over and add it back to the "earth"—that is, the dissolved ice-water—and coagulate it again. This is because the subtle spirits must remain with it; therefore, this coagulation must be done very gently.

But if no spirits have risen during the coagulation, you should not add the phlegm back to it. Instead, take only the substance described above and coagulate and dissolve it at once, as indicated before. Then this work is prepared, and you have the Mercury of Common Life rightly made as it should be in itself, as mentioned in the *Archidoxis* of Theophrastus <note>Refers to *Archidoxis magica* or the *Archidoxes of the Secrets of Nature* by Paracelsus (Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, 1493–1541).</note>.

# Augmentation of the Mercury of Life <note>original: "Mercurius vitæ"; in early modern chemistry, this usually refers to antimony oxychloride (Powder of Algaroth), a potent medicinal compound derived from antimony.</note>

Take roughly one part of the prepared Mercury of Life and place it in a coated glass flask <note>original: "beschlagen Kolben Glaß"; a glass vessel reinforced with a layer of clay or lute to withstand heat.</note>. Let it solidify slightly until it reaches an oily consistency and until the small ring <note>A crust or residue ring that forms on the glass during heating.</note> becomes visible. Then, add one part of the "frozen ice-water" <note>Referencing the distillate from the previous page, likely antimony trichloride, which is solid at room temperature.</note> into it. Let it be consumed or dissolve therein. Afterward, let it cool slowly by itself, and it will become solidified.

Then, break the glass flask and place the solidified mass <note>original: "Coagulatum"</note> upon a marble slab to dissolve <note>original: "soluieren"; here meaning to deliquesce, or turn into liquid by absorbing moisture from the air.</note>. In this way, the fixed Mercury of Life holds the spirits of the unfixed ice-water so that they do not evaporate <note>original: "nicht dauon riechen"; literally "do not smell away."</note>. Dissolve and solidify this together in this manner four times, as the process requires. By doing this, you will have a much better Mercury of Life than you had at first, for the spirits that escaped during the first work must thereafter remain joined to it. From this finished work, you may take half—or as much as you wish—to use, and keep the remainder to continue the augmentation.

## USAGE

Its use as a medicine for the human body is as follows: One takes a clean feather quill and dips it into the Mercury of Life. When a drop hangs from the quill, let it fall into the wine described below, ensuring that the correct number of drops are provided for a dose. This should be given to the sick person once a day on an empty stomach, to be drunk every day at 8 o’clock. Afterward, allow the patient to sweat. This should be continued until the sick person has properly regained their health.

The wine in which the Mercury of Life is to be administered should be made from Angelica, Elecampane root <note>original: "Alantwurtzen"; a plant traditionally used for respiratory and digestive ailments.</note>, and Burnet Saxifrage <note>original: "Bibernell"; used in herbal medicine to treat various plagues and inflammatory conditions.</note>.

## Preparation and Sublimation of Gold <note>original: "Solis"; literally "of the Sun," the alchemical symbol for Gold</note>.

Perform this distilling and sublimating three times. On the fourth time, distill only the <term>Phlegm</term> <note>original: "Phlegmam"; the watery, inactive portion of the distillate</note> gently away from it, without the spirits rising. Then pour another 8 lots of <term>Ostrich's Stomach</term> over it and proceed with distilling and sublimating in every way as before. This repetition should occur so often and so many times until the previously described <term>Ostrich's Stomach</term> (called <term>Virgin’s Milk</term>) has all been applied to the 4 lots of <term>Gold</term> <note>original: "Solis"</note>, and driven and sublimated so long that the entire <term>Body of Gold</term> <note>original: "Corpus Solis"</note> has given itself to the air and has sublimated upward.

This is the **Red Tincture**, with which you may tinge silver and all other metals, and also **Red Mercury** <note>original: *Rohten Mercurium*; likely referring to a specific state of mercury after being processed with the tincture</note>, and transform them into a true, solid gold. After the tingeing, it should also be refined in lead until the "glance" <note>original: *Blick*; the sudden flash of light on the surface of molten metal during assaying that indicates all impurities have been removed and the metal is pure.</note> appears, etc.

The Masters of Nature say: this tincture is Black at the beginning, White in the middle, and after the Whiteness, it becomes Red or gold-colored with a strong fire.

Another philosopher says this: The heat working within the moisture produces a blackness at first; and the blackness works into the dryness, so it produces a whiteness; and thereafter, with a great fire, it becomes yellow. After that, if one strengthens the fire even more, it is brought into the beautiful redness, and it is fixed and gold-colored. It is called **Coral** <note>original: *Corallium*</note>, the Red Corals; and it is called the overflowing **Red Sulphur** <note>original: *Rubeum sulphuris*</note>, the **Red Orpiment** <note>original: *Rubeum auripigmentum*; or *Operment*. A mineral traditionally used as a pigment, here referring to a specific alchemical stage.</note>. In this way, the philosophers have given names to this Tincture or Elixir.

Furthermore, one should note this praiseworthy **Medicine** or remedy for the human body, with which all physical illness may be driven away with this powerful Tincture.

Furthermore, there are several fools who say they can make **Potable Gold** <note>original: *Aurum potabile*; a legendary alchemical medicine made of gold dissolved into a liquid form, believed to be a universal cure-all.</note> from common gold alone; and they say it is also the best medicine to heal all diseases. There are also several doctors who are so deceitful that they say it is the best for healing all sicknesses. This is all against nature and is not true **Potable Gold**. They also say it is quite good for the sick person to buy it, and then one should show the gold to the sick person, for looking at the gold serves the sick...

<header>Process</header>

### Method of proceeding in the preparation of the Philosophers' Stone. <note>original Latin: *Modus procedendi in præparatione lapidis Philosophici*</note>

The following treatise was given to me in Nuremberg by Paul Großman; it is said to originate from someone who lived in Erfurt, who truly was supposed to have been able to make the certain **tincture** <note>the "tincture" is the alchemical substance capable of transforming base metals into gold or silver</note>. However, whether everything is to be practiced exactly **to the letter** <note>original: *ad Litterã*</note>, I do not know.

->In the name of the Almighty, begin fortunately to complete your work.<-

First, make **aqua regia** <term>aquam regis: "royal water," a highly corrosive acid mixture used to dissolve noble metals</term> from one part yellow **calcined vitriol** <note>vitriol (sulfates) heated until reduced to a dry powder</note> and one part **saltpeter**. Set it up as you know how, and drive it through an **alembic** <term>alembicum: a beak-like vessel used in distillation</term> for 24 hours, so that the **caput mortuum** <note>literally "dead head"; the dregs or useless residue left in the flask after distillation</note> burns itself out nice and dry. Into this water, put a fourth part **sal ammoniac** <term>salarmoniac: ammonium chloride, often used to help dissolve gold</term>, set it upon warm sand, and let it dissolve. After that, draw off the **phlegm** <term>phlegmam: the watery, inactive portion of a distilled liquid</term> in a **water bath** <term>balneo: a vessel of hot water used for gentle heating</term> as you know how. 

Next, take fine **gold** cast through **antimony** <term>Antimonium: a metalloid used as a flux to purify gold by separating it from other metals</term>, very fine and pure. Granulate it or laminate it into thin sheets, as much as you require. Dissolve it in this water. When it is completely dissolved, draw the water off again through an **alembic** until the water stands in the **water bath** and begins to become thick, so that one cannot easily see through it. Then take it out and place it in a cellar; let it stand for one to four days until beautiful **crystals** form. When that has happened, pour the remaining water off and place it back in the cellar, and let more crystals form. Do this until no more crystals will form.

Afterward, take these crystals of **gold** ☉ <note>the alchemical symbol for Gold</note> or **silver** ☽ <note>the alchemical symbol for Silver</note> and put them into a vial with a long neck, and then take the same weight of **sal ammoniac-**

<header>For the tincture,</header>

[sal am]moniac, water, and **oil of tartar**, you must first pour them together into a glass and let them **putrefy** <term>putrificieren: a period of "digestion" or decomposition where the substances are allowed to break down and transform through gentle heat</term> in a **water bath** <term>Balneo: a container of warm water used to provide steady, indirect heat</term> for 8 days. Afterward, filter it until it is fine and pure, for it leaves many **dregs** <note>original Latin: *fæces*; the solid waste or impurities that settle at the bottom</note> during the putrefaction. When this has been done, pour the three aforementioned parts together and set them in a water bath to putrefy; however, it is better if it is putrefied in its proper fire, namely in **philosophers’ dung** <term>fimo philosophorum: a traditional alchemical heat source, usually a pile of fermenting horse manure, which provided a low, constant temperature for months</term>. Keep it in such a putrefaction for 40 days, and for as long as it takes until it begins to turn black; the blacker it is, the more it is **corrupted** <note>in alchemy, "corruption" is a positive sign that the old form of the metal is dying so a new, purified form can be born</note>. Small **crystals** may also sprout in the **vial**, but do not take it out before 40 days have passed. Then, make it into a **mercury**, in which mercury the entire mastery of this art is accomplished; for in it, we have everything we desire, etc.

<margin>1</margin>
> For it is certain that every thing is made of that into which it is resolved; but all metals are reduced into **mercury**, or **quicksilver**. Therefore, they were [originally] quicksilver. <note>original Latin: *Certum enim est, quod omnis res est ex eo, in quod resoluitur sed omnia metalla reducuntur in mercurium, seu argentum viuum. For this **mercury** is the beginning, **root**, mother, and origin of all metals, both the perfect <note>Gold and Silver</note> and the imperfect <note>Base metals like Lead or Iron</note>. Know that in it alone the greatest **secrets** <note>original: *secreta*</note> are hidden, <margin>2</margin> and in no other; for in mercury is whatever the wise seek. <note>original Latin: *est enim in mercurio, quicquid quærunt sapientes.*</note>

For **Geber** <note>an influential 8th-century Islamic alchemist, whose Latinized works became the foundation of European alchemy</note> says: it is highly necessary for every lover of this art that he have a whole and steady will in our work, and not take up various things, trying now this and then another. For our art cannot be accomplished in many different things, as it is **one stone**, **one medicine**, and is not composed of any external things; rather, we cast away its excess during its preparation.

# Process

Therefore, every person in this Art must be steadfast and attend to his work with gentleness and without any anger, and not abandon the work they have begun until they reach the perfect end.

Therefore, every seeker of this Art should know the beginnings and the root of the nature and manner of our Art or Work; for whoever does not know the beginning cannot come to the end. And I shall reveal the beginning to you in quite clear speech, so that you know how to conduct yourself in all your undertakings: <note>original: "Fac fixum volatile, & volatile fixum, & nisi fiant corpora incorporea, & econuerso, nihil efficies."</note> **Make the fixed volatile, and the volatile fixed, and unless the bodies become incorporeal, and vice versa, you shall achieve nothing.**
<margin>3</margin>

Once it has **putrefied** <term>Putrificiert: a stage of chemical digestion where the substance breaks down, often turning black, to prepare for purification</term> for forty days, take it out and open the **vial** <term>Viol: a glass phial or vessel used for containing the alchemical mixture</term> again. Pour it all together into a clean glass bowl, and pour distilled warm rainwater over it to thoroughly wash away the **salts** <term>salia: mineral or crystalline residues</term> from one another. Do this in the most subtle way; note well that you must wash the salts away cleanly, otherwise, everything will be thrown into a heap <note>that is, the process will fail or the substances will fuse incorrectly</note> during the **sublimation** <term>Sublimieren: heating a substance until it vaporizes and then re-solidifies in a pure form at the top of the vessel</term>. Therefore, you must perform this washing with all diligence.

Once the **salts** have been thoroughly washed away, place the bowl with the material on warm sand and make it quite dry and as parched as possible. When that is done, put the material into a long, coated sublimation flask—the longer, the better. Place a **still-head** <term>Helm: the "helmet" or alembic top of a still where the vapors collect and condense</term> on top, but do not seal it with lute yet. Place it in a **sand-cupel** <term>Capell: a sturdy container filled with sand to provide indirect, even heat—a sand bath</term> and give it just a little fire, so that the sand only begins to get warm for six hours. After that, strengthen the fire a little for another six hours; then stronger again for six hours; and for the final six hours, maintain the heat so that even the sand at the bottom of the cupel glows.

When you have thus sublimated the material for twenty-four hours, let the glass cool thoroughly. Then take out the sublimated material, carefully placing it into a fine glass bowl, and pour a little good distilled wine vinegar over it

# Process

...around the glass, between the sphere, there must be three cross-fingers <note>approx. 2.25 inches</note> of empty space all around the glass, so that the vapors and heat can move one another. And also note this secret concerning the wooden sphere: the bottom half, upon which it shall stand, must be full of holes all around the circumference to about two cross-fingers from the bottom center. The holes should be approximately large enough for a large cherry pit to fall through. The other half must be solid and have no holes, so that this vaporous heat can operate correctly according to nature.

Now take such a sphere together with the glass in which the matter stands, and place it in its fire—namely, in dung <note>original: "Fimum," a horse-manure bath used in alchemy to provide a gentle, constant, and natural heat</note>, as you will be taught later. Then the Mercury <term>Mercury [☿]</term> inside begins, after eight or more days, to open itself up due to the vaporous mists and steady heat; and from day to day it gradually dissolves—which the movable, steady heat accomplishes—and through such means, the Mercury <term>Mercury [☿]</term> dissolves into its own water. And that which is dissolved becomes airy <note>original: "lustig," meaning it takes on the properties of air or volatility</note> and gradually rises into its own sphere to elevate itself, settling at the top in the circumference of the glass like dew—yet not all at once, but so slowly that one can hardly perceive it.

(Arnoldus <margin>S</margin> says in his *Rosarium*: "In our work, putrefaction is necessary because nothing ever grows, neither plants nor animals, except after putrefaction, etc. For if there is no putrefaction, it cannot be dissolved, and if it is not dissolved, it is reduced to nothing. Therefore, our putrefaction is neither filthy nor unclean, but is the co-mingling of water with earth.") <note>original: "sua Rosario dicit in opere nostro putrefactio est necessaria..." Arnold of Villanova was a famous 13th-century alchemist; the *Rosarium Philosophorum* is a seminal alchemical text.</note>

For first, the water dissolves the body, which happens because of the oil; therefore it is called an **unctuous vapor** <term>Unctuous vapor [Vapor vnctuosus], a heavy, oily mist</term>, which mist is heavier to rise than the water. The water dissolves, the air sublimes, the fire liquefies...

### For the Tincture

<margin>6</margin>
The Earth coagulates <note>original: "Coaguliert"; the process of a liquid becoming solid</note>, so that the four elements bring forth their effect through the medium of heat, and each one hastens to its duty for the swiftest generation; thus the Body is brought through itself, as has been said: It dissolves <note>original: "Soluiert"</note> itself, and makes itself living, and kills itself without ceasing; <note>original Latin: "in eo fiunt omnes modi, scilicet sublimatio, distilatio, solutio, coagulatio, fixatio, &c."</note> in it all modes occur, namely: sublimation, distillation, dissolution, coagulation, fixation, etc. Therefore our crushing <note>original Latin: "contritio"; usually a manual grinding, but here referring to the chemical breakdown</note> should not be done with hands, but by the strongest boiling <note>original Latin: "decoctione"</note>.

<margin>7</margin>
All of this is done by Nature alone, through the medium of her steady heat, which drives the natural elements forward so that they may be separated in their transformation; for they do not truly depart from one another, so that the separation is nothing other than a transformation of one into the other: out of the Water, Air shall be born; out of the Air, the Fire; out of the Fire, again the Earth. (Aristotle: <note>original Latin: "Cum habueris aquam ex aere, aerem ex igne, ignem ex terra, tunc habebis plenam artē."</note> When you have the water from the air, the air from the fire, and the fire from the earth, then you will have the full art.) For they are not separated [permanently], but for the sake of the transformation it is called a separation; also, Nature fixes <note>original: "figiert"; becomes stable, solid, and resistant to fire</note> herself back together without any discord, so that in this Work, Body, Soul, and Spirit are separated; for the Spirit is the seat and housing of the Soul, wherein she rests.

For the moisture from the Spirit is like water, and the moisture from the Soul is like oil (<note>original Latin: "vapor vnctuosus est lapis noster"</note> an oily vapor <term>Unctuous vapor</term> <note>A thick, fatty mist or steam considered the "glue" that binds the alchemical spirit and body</note> is our stone); therefore the Soul is in the bonds of the Spirit, just as the body is a bond of the Soul; yet the [human] bond is nothing compared to the bond of Nature.

<margin>8</margin>
<note>original Latin: "Tota operatio nostra non est aliud nisi extractio aquæ à terra, & huius aquæ super terram dimissio, donec terra putrefiat. Hæc enim terra cum aqua putrefit & mundificatur: Cum mundata fuerit, auxilio diuinitatis totū magisterium perficitur."</note> Our entire operation is nothing other than the extraction of water from the earth, and the pouring of this water back upon the earth, until the earth putrefies. For this earth putrefies and is purified with the water: When it has been purified, the whole mastery <note>original: "magisterium"; the finished alchemical Great Work</note> is perfected with the help of the divine. And elsewhere: <note>original Latin: "Spiritus domini ferebatur super aquas."</note> The Spirit of the Lord was carried over the waters.

For just as in the creation of the world, first there was the Water, and the Spirit of God hovered over it,

# Process

<margin>9</margin>
Thus it is also at the beginning of this work in the sublimation <note>The process of heating a substance until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again</note>; for it performs an upward and downward work until it has entirely dissolved <note>original: "Soluiert"</note> its Body into a beautiful, transparent water, just like crystal. Our water is nothing other than a vapor or mist, which is called Air, and has gradually risen into the heights, moving from the corporeal water into the roundness of the sphere, like the dew. *The wind carried it in its belly* <note>original Latin: "Portauit illum ventus in ventre suo"; a famous line from the Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus</note> and elsewhere. *For it ascends from the earth to the heaven, and again descends to the earth, and receives the power of the superiors and the inferiors.* But through the long action and steady, unceasing heat of its rising and falling, it becomes slightly thicker over time. However, understand that this does not happen quickly; for the whole Body must first have been in the height of its circle, then it becomes and begins to grow thicker and browner. And if it should happen that something of the Body remains, it eventually consumes it, so that it becomes spiritual. And I tell you in the Divine Truth that the Art is nothing other than dissolving and coagulating <note>original: "Soluieren vnnd Coagulieren"</note> the Stone, which happens through putrefaction <note>original: "Putrefaction"; the chemical breakdown or "rotting" of the substance required for rebirth</note> alone.

<margin>10</margin>
*The craftsman <note>original Latin: "Artifex"</note> of our work must first dissolve the stone, then coagulate it, since our work is nothing other than making a perfect solution and coagulation elsewhere. Unless everything is changed from earth into water, one can in no way reach perfection elsewhere. Namely, both of these—the dissolution of the body and the coagulation of the spirit—will be in one operation, and one does not happen without the other. Therefore gold and silver are dissolved; to dissolve the body and coagulate the spirit is the work of ripening.*

<margin>11</margin>
Know also that the solution and coagulation are distinct, yet they have only a single operation—namely, the medium of heat. For as soon as it has dissolved, it has also completed its coagulation. *If you have diligently inspected the wisdom of these sayings, you will easily be able to know it; for they said of it: that this disposition is the change of nature and of things.*

### For the Tincture

...and a subtle arrangement and wonderful mixing of the natural properties of heat and moisture with cold and dryness.

This is that arrangement which cannot be perfected by hands <note>original: "manibus perfici non potest"; implying it is a natural or divine process that occurs within the vessel rather than through manual manipulation</note>.

When you now see here that everything begins to stand still at the bottom and no longer rises, then Nature has completed the union <term>conjunction|the alchemical "marriage" or unification of opposing substances, such as spirit and body</term>, for it becomes ever thicker. Then the elements, along with the soul, joined with the spirit, unite the spiritual body back into one; it is an incombustible oil <term>oleum incombustibile|a legendary alchemical substance that can endure fire without being consumed, signifying perfect stability</term>. And if you dip a glowing Moon <note>symbol for silver</note> into this oil, it will immediately turn into the Sun <note>symbol for gold</note>. However, there is no need to open your glass vessel if you truly wish your work to be perfect. For know that this oil no longer loses its various parts, because gold is nothing other than a prepared fixed oil <note>original: "fix oleum præparatum"</note> that can suffer no injury in the fire. Therefore, the extracted richness <note>original: "feettigkeit", literally "fatness"—referring to the oily, combustible essence of a substance</note> of the oil is a tincture <term>tincture|a potent liquid or "medicine" used to transform base metals into noble ones</term>, for the richness belongs to the soul, which is extracted with great difficulty, but rather very slowly and subtly, just as all the philosophers write.

<margin>12</margin>
Its temperament is balanced and its nature is directed in heat, cold, moisture, and dryness; you will find nothing in it that is superfluous nor anything diminished. Let air nourish the fire, just as water nourishes the earth; fix the earth and the water so that the air can be fixed into the water. For if you have well "killed" the water, you have also "killed" the elements, and they are dead <note>In alchemy, to "kill" or "mortify" a substance is to destroy its external form so that its inner essence can be reborn in a higher state</note>.

<margin>13</margin>
When the oil has thus become lemon-brown <note>original: "Citrin braun"</note> in its fire, it takes on a fiery nature, ready to ignite itself, and it penetrates what was hidden in its interior at the beginning. And so this is the cause of retaining the water and the air in the oil against combustion, and the oil is the cause of retaining the tincture of the moisture, which is the cause of the appearance of the colors. Thus, it will bring the thick into the subtle, and the water will want to strive against the fire and yet endure the same.

<margin>14</margin>
And if you understand well, here lies our whole philosophy; and it should be noted that in the hidden part of our stone is heat and dryness, and...

# Processus
# <note>Process</note>

In the manifest [outward state] there is coldness and humidity, wherefore it is necessary to hide its manifest state; and the heat, which is in the hidden state, is the element oil, which is dry. For this dryness fixes, and the dryness of the fire tints. However, that which is manifest is coldness and humidity; it is necessary, therefore, to have a proportion between them, so that coldness and humidity are tempered by the heat and dryness which were hidden. That certain coldness and humidity is an aqueous and burnt smoke <note>original: "fumus aquosus & adustus"</note>, which corrupts and gives birth to blackness <note>This refers to the *Nigredo* or "blackening" stage, where the material is broken down and purified through symbolic death or decay.</note>. And that Stone <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note> is of one virtue and nature in the hidden state, and of another in the manifest; but in a complete mixture, it is of the same virtue and nature. And thus the Spirit is changed into a most noble Body, then it becomes flowing and an Oil, which is the true Tincture: multiplicative <note>able to increase the quantity of gold or medicine</note>, consolidating, warming, clarifying, purifying, and confirming.

Note that this oil at first stands above the water, and when it happens to thicken, it finally and slowly falls to the bottom. In color, it is like lily-brown <note>likely referring to a deep, reddish-brown color similar to certain spotted lilies or the "Martagon" lily</note> or like pomegranate skins. Then know that you must henceforth govern the vaporous [fumes] well without ceasing and not let them be still, to renew them after the fifth day, as you will be taught later regarding the furnace. And finally, when the <term>Fixation|the alchemical process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to heat</term> begins, a little skin will form upon the oil, which from day to day becomes deeper and deeper. It also finally falls quite slowly to the bottom like a yellow, subtle sand, and this becomes more and more visible until it has all fallen. Let it stand thus in its warmth, and it will begin to slowly turn gray-black. So give it its fire continually, until it turns away from the black color again and changes into a pure, clear whiteness. And when the true whiteness <note>The *Albedo* stage, representing the second major goal of the work: the creation of the White Stone or White Elixir</note> arrives, you will see all kinds of wonderful colors in the glass, like little streams rising from the matter; as soon as one has barely passed, another takes its place.

# Effects of the water.

<margin>15</margin>
Our water <note>original: "Aqua nostra"; refers to the alchemical solvent or "mercury of the philosophers"</note> mortifies, illuminates, cleanses, and brings to life. It causes black colors to appear first during the mortification [decay] of the Body, while it is being converted into earth. After the middle stage, many and varied colors appear before the whitening; the end of all these is whiteness <note>original: "albedo"; the second major stage of the Great Work</note>. However, in the mixing of the Water and the Body of the prepared ferment, infinite colors appear. Thus it is apparent that there is one mastery, from one thing and with one thing; and thus from four and three, one <note>This likely refers to the four elements and the three principles (Salt, Sulfur, Mercury) being unified into the Stone</note>. Likewise, the whitening is the beginning of the work and the foundation of the whole Body; from then on, it does not change into various colors except for red <note>original: "rubeum"; the "Rubedo" or final stage</note>, which is the ultimate end.

<margin>X</margin>
When you now see that it is completely snow-white, then you have the Noble True White Philosophical Stone for the white work. Note here a great secret <note>original: "Secretum"</note>: when you have thus completed your Medicine for the white work with the help of the Almighty, you must arrange 1,000 parts of Lime of the Moon <note>original: "Calcis Lunae"; this is silver that has been reduced to a powder through calcination</note> for one part of the Medicine. 
<margin>X</margin>
For these 1,000 parts of lime, take only one part of your white Medicine and rub them well together on a smooth, fine grinding stone. Put all of this together into a well-luted <note>sealed with "lute," a heat-resistant clay or paste</note> crucible <note>original: "Tigel"</note> and place it in a wind-furnace <note>a furnace that uses a draft to reach high temperatures</note>. Give it a moderate fire so that the crucible glows brown for three days and three nights continuously. When that is done, then give it a strong fire and let it flow [melt] for three hours. Then note that no Medicine—even if it has been brought to its philosophical power and perfection—will enter into any metal, neither the perfect nor the imperfect bodies, without the "medium" <note>an intermediary substance or process that allows the medicine to bond with the metal</note>. For the entry must happen through the medium; because even if the Medicine is thrown onto molten metal without the medium and left to melt for ten years, it still will not enter without the aforementioned medium.

# The Process

...ly <note>original: "ein /", continuing the sentence from the previous page: "...purely"</note>. Because of its great purity, it floats on top like an oil upon the water. And note well this great secret, as was previously mentioned: the Medicine glows brown for three days and nights and does not allow itself to melt until those three days and nights have passed. For if it were to melt [for the full] three days and nights, the Medicine would be so penetrative that it would pass right through the crucible <note>alchemical vessels were often porous; a medicine with high "penetration" was thought to be able to seep through solid clay or ceramic if not controlled</note>. Finally, when it has flowed for three hours as mentioned, let it cool by itself. Break the crucible and take it out; it will be as brittle as glass, for it is still a Medicine <note>In this context, "Medicine" refers to the concentrated alchemical substance before it has been diluted or "multiplied" into metal</note>.

Then take the melted white <gloss>medicine</gloss> <note>original: "medicinæ"</note> and cast it again upon 1,000 parts of <term>tin <note>original symbol: ♃ (Jupiter)</note></term> or <term>copper <note>original symbol: ♀ (Venus)</note></term> when it is in a state of flux [melted]. It then tinctures all these 1,000 parts into eternally fine, stable <term>silver <note>original: "Lunam" (the Moon)</note></term>.
